speaker: The Chairman
text: Head L, Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head L of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MSE's portfolio is a broad but incredibly crucial one.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As long as we breathe, eat and live in Singapore, MSE's policies touch all our lives and we have an important goal of ensuring sustainability at the heart of everything we do.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The goals and efforts in the green plan are ambitious but I hope that the green plan will set a minimum standard that we will far exceed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Earth needs us to achieve and then go beyond the Green Plan.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Green Plan should be a living document that we can continuously review and update from now until 2030.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We can afford to move the base line upwards and expect higher standards of our sustainability performance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We cannot afford to rest on our laurels once we meet the existing target.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ultimately, we need to remember that the goal is not to check off every target in the Green Plan.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The goal is to slow down, stop and reverse if possible, Earth's path towards widespread and irreversible climate collapse.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope our conversations about the Green Plan over the next decade will both be about how we can meet the targets and what higher targets we will be shedding for ourselves.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For this Committee of Supply, my Government Parliamentary Committee colleagues, fellow Members of Parliament and I will be asking lots of questions and making numerous suggestions for sustainability and MSE's other portfolios.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will MSE work with industry and civil society to strengthen the Green Plan?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will MSE shore up climate resilience by enhancing coastal protection and boosting flood resilience?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will MSE strengthen the resilience of our food supply and ensure food safety?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will MSE strengthen Singapore's water security by greening our water treatment processes and increasing water efficiency?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will MSE work towards a zero waste nation by closing the e-waste, packaging waste and food waste loop?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will MSE build a clean and endearing home for all by raising public health standards, transforming our environmental services industry and sustaining the hawker industry?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are lots more questions, and Madam, I look forward to a robust debate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Race to the bottom of the amount of carbon emitted.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The European Union, Japan and the Republic of Korea, together with more than 110 other countries, have pledged carbon neutrality by 2050.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Of course, commitments must be back by ambitious action and concrete plans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But setting a goal is invaluable in itself.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: First, it sends a clear signal to its industries, citizens and civil society on the direction and speed of policy change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The signal will have a trickle down effect in influencing decisions in boardrooms and individual action.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Second, it provides a yardstick for measuring if we are taking bold enough actions to achieve our declared goals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The Government introduced the Public Service Taking The Lead in Environmental Sustainability (PSTLES) initiative back in 2006.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: During Committee of Supply last year, PMO announced that it intends to raise its ambitions and for the next phase of the initiative.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Can the Ministry share some of its plans and targets?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Under current initiative, each Ministry is required to appoint a Sustainability Manager to set sustainability targets for FY2020 and to develop a resource management plan to meet its targets.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In addition to the reporting in the Singapore Public Sector Outcomes Review, will the Government consider requiring Sustainability Managers to publicly report annually how well their Ministries have fared in achieving targets set for their Ministries?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Also, many countries have emphasised the importance of a green recovery, even as the world continues to reel from the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: What are the Public Service's own plans on environmental sustainability and how does it intend to decarbonise?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Singapore has to play our part to reduce carbon emissions and adapt to the impact of climate change.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have deep interest in the global efforts to fight the deteriorating effects of climate change and Singapore has been an active player and strong supporter of multilateral approaches to tackle climate challenges.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Given our limited access to renewable energy, our pledge towards the Paris Agreement is indeed an ambitious one.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, I understand that countries like US, European Union, Japan, South Korea and China and among others have set even more ambitious targets and have declared that they would reach net zero emission or carbon neutrality by 2050 or 2060.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the light of these developments, can I ask would Singapore be raising its climate change ambitions further?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: How we gear up our economy and the society towards carbon neutrality and how long would it take realistically?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This would make solar energy as one of the "Four Energy Switches" for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Government has accelerated efforts to harness solar energy via increased deployment of solar panels and energy storage solutions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We are also gearing up industry players to scale up capabilities and to stay abreast of the latest solar technological developments.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In Singapore context, the key limitations to solar being one of our major sources of energy are our lack of vast spaces and the fluctuating cloud cover due to our weather.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Other than HDB blocks, can I ask the Minister what are the examples of untapped spaces that the Government intends to deploy solar, and how is the Government leveraging innovation to do so?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Besides solar, can I also seek an update from the Minister on the key efforts and initiatives that the Government is working on with the private sector?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is part of the plan to strengthen the regional grid architecture and allow countries to share clean energy sources.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I ask the Minister how will this impact electricity prices and what are the considerations the Government will take into account to manage price volatility?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: How can consumers play a part in this transition, and how does the Government intend to support them?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many issues need our attention and urgent action.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But funds and resources are limited, and have been further strained due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore needs to select and decide on our climate goals and achievable milestones.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are a small city state with a densely built urban environment and manufacturing facilities, as well as an air, maritime and financial hub.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, our carbon emissions are not insignificant relative to our geographical size.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yet, we are dependent on these activities to survive as we lack natural resources.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can we balance these competing demands and meet our short and long-term climate goals without compromising the quality of life for our citizens?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Minister elaborate on our climate initiatives and projects?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What can we achieve in the short, medium and long term together with the communities in the world?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond mitigating our domestic emissions, how can Singapore contribute to international efforts to achieve Singapore's climate goals?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need a whole-of-society approach to solve the problem of carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We also use a lot of air-conditioning in our hot and humid weather.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How do we incentivise companies to make more efficient use of electricity?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Thirdly, we need to encourage our people to use more public transportation to cut down on emissions from private vehicles.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Emissions are also linked to our diets and lifestyles.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Eating less meat and reducing waste will make a lot of difference.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The global momentum on climate change has accelerated significantly with many countries increasing that climate ambitions.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As a responsible global citizen, we are doing our part to fight against climate change and commit to fulfilling our pledge.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The targets of the Singapore Green Plan 2030 includes lowered carbon emissions, creating green spaces and investment in green technology.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Embarking on these initiatives will require several trade-offs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: For example, setting space for solar panels might limit space for other activities.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As Singapore works towards achieving our climate targets, what are the other anticipated trade-offs and how are we addressing them?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Singapore needs to continue to remain attractive for investments.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our lower tax rates compared to other developed countries is one of the many reasons that makes us attractive for investments.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will it encourage the industry to adopt new technologies to be more efficient or will it reduce our attractiveness for investments as investors look for cheaper and less restrictive alternatives in this region?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Hany Soh, please take your three cuts together.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In recent months, I have participated in a series of dialogue sessions, both formal and informal ones, involving people from all walks of life, including my Woodgrove residents, both young and old.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: All of them spoke with great enthusiasm in advocating for a greener society.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am therefore heartened with the recent launch of the Singapore Green Plan 2030.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this regard, I wish to ask the Ministry, how can Singaporeans take part in this important Green Plan effort?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To succeed in our Singaporean Green Plan 2030, I see the need to collectively and continuously involved the efforts of our "Three Ps": People, Private and Public sectors.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What kind of programmes will the Ministry introduced to foster more collective actions by the Three Ps to combat climate change together?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What is the target outcome that we are trying to achieve from each of these programmes for the next three, five and 10 years?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Which of the programmes would be expected to have the most impact in a community, in the business community and for the individuals respectively?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As shared in the recent debate on the Motion to accelerate and deepen efforts against climate change, the community in Woodgrove would like to work closely with the relevant agencies and private sectors, to participate as a community to achieve the greatest impact in combating climate change for the better well-being of our future generations.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In terms of involving the community, I understand that the SG Eco Fund was launched last year to support projects that advance environmental sustainability and promote the community's involvement.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And thirdly, what is the desired outcome for each project supported by the SG Eco Fund?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I hope that these projects are able to achieve sustainable outcomes and be scalable in scope, allowing them to be easily replicated and introduced across Singapore in the long run.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I also hope that one of the key aspects would be the tap on this projects to nurture more individuals as green champions for our community.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have recently watched a screening of "A Wicked Problem", a climate change documentary series by CNA hosted by Senior Minister of State for MCI, Dr Janil, in which he hits the ground to investigate what Singapore is doing to combat climate change and to rally Singaporeans to do their part in their personal capacities.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I hope that MCI will track and gather feedback from viewers the impact and the outcome of such documentary series.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I personally find such programmes engaging and insightful and hope that more of them can be created in other languages and even dialects to raise more awareness and support for Singaporeans to come together to combat climate change.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With effect like this, we can make a difference for the greener benefit of our future generations.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In Mandarin):    The Singapore Green Plan 2030 is jointly led by the MOE, MND, MSE, MTI and MOT to set clear goals for urban greening, sustainable living and green finance.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But I think that MCI, as the Ministry responsible for ICT, media, government information and public communication strategies, plays an important supportive role in driving the public sector, businesses and Singaporeans towards the goal of sustainable development in the next 10 years.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I hope that the MCI will launch a series of programmes in four languages as well as various dialects to encourage Singaporeans to participate more in sustainable living.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: By adopting the ‘listening more and watching more’ approach, I hope that Singaporeans will understand that it is everyone's responsibility to protect the Mother Earth and green up the environment.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I firmly believe that as long as our people stay united and do their part to combat climate change, our next generation will have a better green future.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, apart from some of these, the Green Plan mostly outlines many existing initiatives and targets that were previously already announced.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To demonstrate our seriousness on treating climate change as a global emergency and existential threat that it is today, we need to continue pushing the boundaries and set bold and vicious targets for ourselves.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There is room for us to strive for even more.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In addition, will the Government consider setting a more specific deadline to reach net zero emissions, taking into consideration IPCC's recommendation of net zero by 2050?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: They had the courage to dream big, creating a “First World oasis in a Third World region”, and the leadership to make it happen.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Their rallying cry was for this “mudflat to become a metropolis”!

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: When they look at what we have here today, they should feel that their sweat and tears are justified.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We hope that when it is our turn to look at where we would have brought Singapore to, we too, will be justified.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Climate change is a global emergency and a threat to mankind.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to focus this cut on the business of climate change and the business of the SGP.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The global crisis presents an opportunity for Singapore to be the world's living laboratory for all things smarter and sustainable.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For a start, many of our SMEs do not understand how all this will impact them.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How will MSE and the whole-of-Government help our companies to begin their journey, starting with awareness?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Next, companies will need to know where they are and what steps they need to take to get to the green standards that will be expected.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There will be new skills and new jobs.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Our workers and our future workforce will need to be trained as well.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How will education and CET curriculum in our schools and IHLs change to reflect this future?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In closing, I believe that there is a unique opportunity for Singapore businesses to create a vibrant value chain eco-system and circular economy around this Singapore Green Plan 2030 movement.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: With SGP 2030, it is once in a lifetime or last in a lifetime opportunity for the business community, the Government, academia, experts to begin the dialogue and co-create an integral development approach to economic and social growth, bringing everyone along. "The future forward begins now.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We only need to imagine it, to decide it and to do it”.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The Singapore Green Plan 2030 that is organised along five pillars and outlined by the five Ministries is, indeed, encouraging.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I would also like to know, how can we emerge from the COVID-19 pandemic with a greener and more sustainable future for Singapore?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Would the Minister for Sustainability and Environment shed light on these queries?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Residents can expect transformations which will enhance their environments so that there will be more sustainable and livable space for residents.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On the drawing board are sustainable community touchpoints such as hawker centres which will have zero waste by composting food scraps.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, these towns will be able to track their energy consumption, water usage, carbon emissions and their progress in recycling.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on what has been implemented so far and what future developments can be expected?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will new waste disposal methods such as Pneumatic Waste Conveyance System be introduced in these towns?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Prof Koh Lian Pin, you can take your three cuts together.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: One of these initiatives is City in Nature.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: These are ambitious and important targets for transforming Singapore into an even greener and more beautiful city by 2030.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Ministry share its plans for tracking progress towards achieving these targets over the next decade?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, more importantly, what does success look like in terms of the outcomes of City in Nature for the public, private and people sectors?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Green spaces are important for the many benefits they provide to Singapore.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: These benefits may include conserving biodiversity, addressing climate change impacts, and improving the physical and mental health of our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: The success of City in Nature in delivering these outcomes, hinges not just on the amount of additional green spaces that we set aside to meet our target, but also on the quality of these green spaces, with respect to the different benefits we hope to derive from them.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, our understanding of the different types and values of green spaces could be a matter for public consultation and discussion, as part of the Green Plan Conversations.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: The Green Plan Conversations are a timely and constructive opportunity for the public, private and people sectors to take a holistic approach in considering what should be part of Singapore’s current natural resources and future natural heritage.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: These Conversations are also an important opportunity for the public, private and people sectors to communicate even more effectively with one another to strengthen our mutual trust and social compact, as we manage the inevitable and growing tensions between economic development and nature conservation in Singapore.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: For example: Perhaps, the Government could explain more plainly to the people why it cannot ease the demand for land, if that is indeed the case.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, the nature community could explain more convincingly to the Government why green spaces should be valued as our natural capital and national assets.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: And perhaps, all of us could demonstrate that we can take a pragmatic, calibrated and science-based approach to face our challenges, make hard decisions and co-create solutions as a society.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: I think most Singaporeans do appreciate that there are multiple priorities, constraints and trade-offs that need to be considered in making our urban planning decisions.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: On the other hand, as a biophilic, or nature-loving, society, many of us wish to hold on to every little piece of remaining greenery we understand to be relatively pristine.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: That is why the public, private and people sectors may also benefit from having the bigger picture of what remains of our green spaces in Singapore to help frame our discussions and align our perspectives and priorities.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: To appreciate this bigger picture may require us to answer a few important questions, including: Where are the green spaces that we must defend at all costs?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Where are the necessary ecological buffers and corridors that we need to protect?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: What other green spaces are there in Singapore, where are they located and what are their marginal values for nature conservation?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: I am confident that this effort to be led by our National Parks Board, in partnership with our academic nature and community stakeholders, will produce invaluable perspectives, science and tools to help inform Singapore's long-term planning decisions.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: The Green Plan conversations are therefore a vital and necessary platform for us to engage in open discussions, consultations and communications to co-create an effective environmental management framework and set of processes for achieving the intended targets and outcomes of the City in Nature initiative and the Singapore Green Plan.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: By working together to consider the green spaces we have left, not in isolation but in their totality, we can make the whole greater than the sum of its parts.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: And upon the completion of those investigations, I am confident that the necessary deterrents and safeguards will be put in place to prevent it from ever happening again.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Apart from the premature clearance at Kranji, I think there are other important issues that may be even more deserving of our attention.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: For example, what must we do to ensure the success of the ecological corridor that would run through the Agri-Food Innovation Park at Kranji, in fulfilling its function of increasing ecological connectivity across Singapore?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: How can we do the same for the other ecological corridors on the island?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, these questions need to be discussed in consultation with the nature and scientific communities.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: I am also happy to learn that the Ministry will continue efforts to strengthen our Environmental Impact Assessment, or EIA, framework.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: EIAs are an essential part of good environmental governance, as they empower and enable the authorities to get the most complete information on a proposed development, through rigorous scientific protocols and engagements with nature and community stakeholders.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: A centralised EIA approach could help reduce the risk of any conflict of interest, increase and maintain EIA standards and eliminate any ad-hoc and inconsistent practices.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps another improvement for the Ministry to consider is to adopt a more precautionary approach in our EIA framework.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: At the moment, the Ministry and relevant agencies as technical experts, shoulder the initial burden and responsibility of having to assess the likelihood of any environmental impact that may result from development and the need for any environmental studies and mitigation measures.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: I think this preliminary layer of information can add to the context-specific set of considerations that the Ministry and relevant agencies will have to act on as decision-makers.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Ultimately, a sound EIA framework helps to increase transparency in our urban planning decisions, encourage stakeholder participation and ensure greater public support of development plans and mitigation measures at later stages.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: As we continue to discuss and debate the various ways to improve the EIA framework and other key ingredients of good environmental governance, we should not lose sight of the overarching goals and outcomes that the public, private and people sectors all seek to achieve.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: I believe we all want to maintain public trust in the credibility and integrity of the processes by which we evaluate the different priorities and trade-offs of our society, so that we can make the most informed decisions on our natural capital for the benefit of the current and future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: An example is the Department of Transportation in Toronto, where they take reference on historical rainfall data to forecast peak discharge flows from two of their local basins that had recently experienced severe flooding affecting several highways.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: By adopting climate forecasting and re-modelling of the streamflow, they can estimate future flooding using projected climate data for the region.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: These revised forecasts were then compared to asset inventory, allowing analysis of all transportation infrastructure.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: This enabled the Department to identify at-risk roads, bridges and other infrastructure and include design elements to reduce their vulnerability to future flooding.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The same applies to our infrastructure for goal towards electrification of vehicles.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The conversion rate is highly dependent on public education, access to charging infrastructure, comparable cost and more choices of alternative vehicles.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: There is also need for stronger public-private partnership to establish the full infrastructures on an expedited basis.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Recently, the Government shared that our sustainability measures will include nature-based solutions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Can I ask what are these solutions and how will we support research and development in this area?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: For building designs with lower carbon emissions and for sustainable maintenance, we should incorporate innovative design solutions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: In Singapore’s tropical weather, the strong rain, wind and sun will have an impact on HDB flats and commercial buildings.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Let us take an example – the Marco Polo Tower in Hamburg.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Each floor of the apartment building is sent a few degrees away from the one below, around an axis, which allows for recessed facades that protect residents from direct sun and negates the need for heavy usage of air conditioning.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Another notable green feature of this development is the inclusion of heat exchanger on the roof that turns warm air into a cooling system and natural ventilation that implies residents can sleep soundly without being disrupted by external noise.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Another example is the Shanghai Tower – the world's second tallest building.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: There is a transparent second skin wrapped around the building creating a buffer of captured air that serves as natural ventilation, thus reducing energy costs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Two hundred and seventy wind turbines are also incorporated into the facade to power its exterior lights.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Thanks to measures like these, the tower uses significantly less power than other skyscrapers and has a platinum LEED certification.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on this?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: As we move towards sustainability, there is also a need to ensure our food supply security.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: This means we need to integrate creative ways of farming in our urban landscape to address the food demand under land scarcity condition.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: From re-purposing rooftop of multi-storey carparks, urban farming buildings to agri-farm cluster, there are certainly ways to raise awareness about our security needs and integrate investments.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: We should do more to encourage Singaporeans and local companies to be a part of this effort.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Besides companies, I believe that more can be done on an individual level.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: We can actually begin by changing our habits and focusing on reduction of energy usage, increase the amount of conservation and upcycling.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: NParks's "Gardening with Edibles" initiative during this circuit breaker was well-received, with many still continuing this labour of love for plants and edibles at their home or in the community.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: How can we encourage more residents and enthusiasts to sustain this interest and be part of the green efforts in the community?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Can this attract the younger generation to a new green economy of smart farming.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: I am hopeful that we too can encourage the next generation to sustain and manage the farming industry in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Much has been outlined on a national level for the Singapore Green Plan 2030.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The Green Plan is built upon five key pillars, but it encompasses many aspects of sustainability that we wish to frame our policy and actions upon.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: First a roadmap on job creation for the green economy.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: I have met residents, youths and mid-career individuals who wish to join and they are keen to be part of this green economy.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: However, this being an emerging area meant there is more ambiguity on the type of jobs available and what these jobs are like.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: To better facilitate the creation of a more detailed roadmap and career path for those interested, I have raised some of these in a recent Private Member's Motion on climate change.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: One, to provide more variety in the courses at the Institutes of Higher Learning for those who are interested in the field of sustainability as a career.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Another area is facilitating early or mid-career moves towards jobs focused on environmental sustainability in partnerships with companies through structured mentorship and work transition programmes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: We can also work with industries and public sector to outline the types of future green jobs and constantly align on skills and competencies required for such roles in the emerging sectors.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Singapore has already made huge inroads in green finance and is considered the leader in ASEAN.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: How can we further grow this sector and seize the future opportunities?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Though, it had acknowledged that a complete harmonisation may be too onerous, suggesting something closer to banking regulations where each country's requirements can align with the global rules and allow for greater flexibility in adoption within each of the country.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: And lastly, encouraging ground-up initiatives and collaboration with the Government.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Suggestions were put forth to create an eco-system to adopting a collaborative consultative partnership between citizens, Government and the private sector to address issues pertaining to climate change and the green economy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We have a high concentration of mature flats and are affectionately known as the "chap lao, 十楼".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We now have a comprehensive public transport network, four hawker centres and many other amenities serving our constituency.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I am thankful for what we have, but I also think about how we can sustain high quality living experience for many generations of residents in MacPherson.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is highly disruptive to our residents, especially our seniors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If the lifts are to be replaced entirely before its planned lifecycle, overall costs can increase very significantly as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As we progress, and age, we can expect to see more mature estates and aged infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But to tear down and rebuild everything is also untenable over the long run, quite wasteful as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, we must find solutions to preserve our infrastructure's longevity and maintain the quality of our living environment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The quantum advancement in technology, applied to the digitalisation of energy, can allow us to move from reactive to predictive maintenance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Back to the HDB lift example, leveraging smart technology, data and machine learning enables Town Councils to intervene before the lift breaks down.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This reduces downtime, cuts operational costs and improves customer experience for residents.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And hopefully, cost-savings can be passed on to residents eventually in the form of lower S&CC.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I note that the HDB collaborated with the Imperial College London and A*STAR in 2017 to embark on a research programme to study how smart sensing and analytics strengthen predictive analytics for efficient estate maintenance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: More importantly, what is the Government's plan to leverage smart technology and data to enhance quality living and preserve the tangible and intangible value for estates, especially mature ones like MacPherson?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This difference could be due to many reasons, but a very likely cause is that aged infrastructure can lose efficiency and consume more energy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Perhaps the Ministry could shed some light on this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, I am glad that there are national programmes such as the Solar Nova.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Solar energy is clean and offers cost predictability.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I also believe that by scaling the use of solar energy, the positive environment impact is highly significant.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Unlike new estates where sustainable solutions and green designs can be applied from step 1, it is tougher to "retrofit" mature estates.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But if we can turn these so-called "Brownfields" green by going smart, we would create a real innovative model that others can follow.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This way, we could also retain the distinct identities of our mature estates and keeping them vibrant for generations to come.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Our efforts for a more sustainable Singapore must be in both the hardware and infrastructure we built to fight climate change and also the hardware of Singaporeans – our behaviour, priorities and lifestyle.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Beyond towns through our city, it has also been a year since the Government announced its vision towards becoming a city in nature.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: In my earlier Budget debate speech, I shared my hopes that some recommendations from the Blue Plan can also be incorporated into the Green Plan.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: As an island city-state, our waters and marine environment are also a very important part of our living environment.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Can the Ministry give an update on the progress made, challenges faced, and possible extensions in carrying out this vision?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: And beyond our green spaces, does the Government have further plans to better protect blue spaces in Singapore and integrate this into our city in nature vision?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: As we integrate nature with urban development, we inevitably also encroach into the homes of our Singaporean wildlife.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Human-wildlife tensions are increasing and I am sure many of us have had heart-stopping moments when we see videos of pangolins or otters crossing the road into incoming traffic.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: As we work towards greener towns and improve connectivity in green corridors, how can we better manage human-wildlife tensions and educate the public?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: To inculcate sustainable habits, we have to start from a young age.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Young Singaporeans spend a large part of their formative years in school where educators impart knowledge and shape the values of our youths from a young age.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: We see that every school is a good school, but schools cannot just be good.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: They also need to be meaningful for life.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: A Junior College Economics student can tell you the effects of negative externalities of pollution on the market.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: But if despite having this knowledge, they still do not choose to adjust to a greener lifestyle, that may not be very meaningful.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: I had called for sustainability to be adopted as part of the core curriculum during the climate change Motion, and I am very heartened to hear that the Government is working towards this.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is embarking on the Green Plan 2030 to spearhead the move for sustainable development in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The immense growth potential of the environmental sector will translate into new jobs and industry transformation.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Would there also be an extension of the scholarship to other degrees or diplomas also related to sustainability?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: To ensure this pipeline, I also believe that the process starts from young.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Students should be exposed to green careers from their Secondary school years.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: These could be done through learning journeys, assembly talks and having sustainability issues become more integrated into the education syllabus.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Teachers and parents will also need to be equipped with the knowledge of this growing industry.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This could be part of the present Eco Stewardship programme.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: There is a wide variety of education options with different career pathways.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Many sustainability careers span beyond science and engineering.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Specialised career guidance in these industries could be considered by ensuring that the present career counsellors in Institutes of Higher Learning are also well-versed in them.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: We could consider having experts and professionals to mentor interested students.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Attachments and internships with green companies and organisations could also be offered.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This would, in the end, help channel these students into green jobs to accelerate Singapore's green recovery from the pandemic and our low-carbon transition.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: With a steady increase of talents in the green industry, and a strong robust framework, Singapore can be an education hub for sustainability and attract ASEAN students to build capacity in the region.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: As we work towards building a sustainable Singapore, we can and must do more to promote individual and collective responsibility to care for the environment.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans should be equipped with sound knowledge and awareness of our environmental issues to inculcate in them a deep care for the environment, and eventually champion and encourage their peers to adopt similar habits.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: It is commonly said that values are not only taught, but also caught.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: How can we ingrain in our students the mindset and attitude to always think about practising sustainability?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Efforts to inculcate the sustainability mindset should be ongoing.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: As our students progress to subsequent stages of education, efforts must continue to reinforce habits to reduce energy usage and reduce waste.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: What are some initiatives that MSE is working with the Institutes of Higher Learning to promote the importance of environmental sustainability?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: My experience as a union leader has also taught me the importance of partnerships and how they are key in ensuring better outcomes.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I would therefore also like to ask how MSE intends to engage different stakeholders among the community, parents and industry partners to more effectively inculcate and reinforce sustainability values in our students.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Our schools play a key role in educating students on the importance of green initiatives and playing a role to combat climate change.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: While environmental education is already present in our school curriculum, what more can we do to enhance the teaching and learning of sustainability concepts?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I am glad to hear of MOE's commitment to support the Singapore Green Plan.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: School is the place to inculcate responsible 4Rs habits and how to recycle properly.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Can the Minister share more on MOE's plans in areas beyond curriculum?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: There is no silver bullet and solutions will necessarily be complex.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Number two, there is a part for all Singaporeans – all of us to play and make a real difference, despite our size.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: We can make a difference in Singapore and we can make a difference for the world.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: The Singapore Green Plan also calls for us to nurture the next generation of Singaporeans with the will, knowledge and practical opportunities to protect and steward our environment for generations to come.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Can MOE share further details about its plans to educate our students on sustainability and their role to co-create and jointly own the Singapore Green Plan, and indeed, our whole-of-society movement towards a greener future?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: We have a population of almost a million vehicles in Singapore last year, according to LTA.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Assuming Net-Zero in the vehicle population going forward, we are still looking at almost a million vehicles in Singapore in 2030.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Converting the entire population to electric vehicles will be a huge undertaking.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: It is worth noting that today, there are roughly 90,000 taxis and private hire vehicles on our roads.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: And so for both taxi and private hire businesses, what are the Ministry's strategies to work with these companies to drive sector wide adoption of electric vehicles?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: What are the key principles, and what are some of the key planks that the Ministry is studying and developing, and this could be in terms of licencing requirements or vehicle ownership regime or the mix of charging infrastructure and its availability across both residential and depot settings for example?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, I also echo some concerns Members have raised about our push for Electric Vehicles (EVs), particularly the installation of charging points.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Is there a corresponding 2030 EV adoption target?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Can our power grid and local sub-stations, particularly those located in older HDB estates, cope with this additional load?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Have we factored in the rapid development of EV batteries, particularly the recent revival in swappable battery technology and battery-as-a-service solutions?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Will this make fixed charging points irrelevant in the years to come?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: What were the lessons learnt from the experience of installing BlueSG charging points, which required significant cross-agency collaboration?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The crux lies in the way EV batteries are produced and, perhaps more critically, how they are disposed.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to research papers, recycling useful materials from lithium-ion batteries remains a tedious and risky process.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Placing them in landfills can cause them to explode and is also not a feasible option for land-scarce Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To better address such potential environmental pollution issues, can the Ministry revise the current Vehicular Emissions Scheme to impose a pollution tax on how "green" the EV manufacturer supply chain is instead of focusing on tailpipe emissions?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The car dealer told me that unless I drive long distances, the savings in petrol would not be able to offset the higher costs of the hybrid car.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Otherwise, the average consumer may not want to pay more for a cleaner or greener vehicle if it burns a big hole in his pocket.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We should also look into making more charging points easily available.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Recent media reports suggest that very few condominiums allow the installation of charging points for Electric Vehicles.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And for those condominiums that wish to do so, they need to seek approval at the annual general meeting (AGM) of residents, whereby 75% must approve the installation of the charging station.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Mandate such installation of such charging points because waiting for the condominium to approve the installation at AGMs would take far too long.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Wherever possible, charging points should also be installed on the streets or roads next to parking lots.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: To encourage condominiums, office buildings and HDB estates to set aside space for charging stations, LTA should also consider some form of financial incentives for them.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If so, what is the cost involved to upgrade electrical power?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We not only need charging points for the Electric Vehicles, we also need the chargers to be able to charge the Electric Vehicles quickly.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If it takes too long to fully charge an Electric Vehicle, then consumers may not want to spend the time waiting for their cars to be charged.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: With the current push toward Electric Vehicles, or EVs, in Singapore and the prospect of converting a large fleet of point-to-point vehicles into EVs, the following are my primary concerns.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: For a mass adoption of EVs in Singapore, we need to better incentivise both private and large fleet owners to switch to EVs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: With the enhanced Vehicular Emissions Scheme, or VES, there is a good chance that the cost of EVs will be similar to that of entry-level luxury cars.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: As a large fleet owner, the complete waiver of the Additional Registration Fee, or ARF, is a welcome move.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, the selling price of the EV after the waiver of ARF is still significantly higher than that of a mass market hybrid vehicle, which makes it hard for mass market adoption.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Is MOT prepared to take a further step to waive all statutory charges, including import duty, related to EV?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If so, this will help to further reduce the cost of EVs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The second is the charging time or the maturity of battery technology.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The charging time of EV, ranging from 30 minutes to two hours for the full charge that allows a range of 200 km to 400 km, is a deterrent.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: For cabbies that use the EV over two shifts of driving, they cannot afford overnight charging of eight to 12 hours like other drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Third is the availability of charging facilities in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: While the number of charging stations will balloon to 60,000 by 2030, which would be a strong impetus for EV adoption, a lot of industrial sites cannot afford for us to install a fast charging station.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Would LTA or related authorities be prepared to improve the power infrastructure of industrial buildings so that fleet owners could install more fast charging stations?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We need a charging farm to support a large fleet of EVs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: While much has been done to drive up the adoption of EVs in Singapore, these are some practical concerns which I hope MOT, LTA and other agencies can address.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Ministry elaborate on how it will promote the adoption of EVs to achieve this new target?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Having been used to a wide range of car models run by internal combustion engines, the EVs' range may not be diverse enough to appeal to some potential buyers who consider a list of other attributes in addition to fuel economy and safety.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These include branding, design, tactile driving, feel, and so on.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What if more owners decide to renew the COEs of older cars operating on internal combustion engines?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is also concerns about maintenance and repairs of EVs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Do we have the manpower training programmes in place to equip and certify a new generation of technicians?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: EVs are more expensive than vehicles utilising internal combustion engines even after factoring in the Electric Vehicle Early Adoption Incentive (EEAI) and enhanced Vehicular Emissions Scheme (VES) incentives.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will the Government make EVs more accessible to all car owners?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Families with young children and the elderly may find these higher priced vehicles a burden, similarly, for those who depend on driving private vehicles for a living.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am also concerned about families with members who have special needs or disabilities who depend on private vehicles for mobility.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Government consider assisting them with family-friendly or disability-related rebates?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How about the maintenance and repairs of EVs?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Does the Government have any indicative figures of such costs and what measures will be introduced to help bring these costs to affordable levels?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am concerned over whether we may be overbuilding, given that the initial adoption rate of EVs may not be as high what as we hope for.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As this may require extensive electrical upgrades, how will the Government reach this target?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will the Ministry ensure that the charging points are well distributed while keeping costs manageable and the final bill to the users affordable?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The other worry is that EVs will be popular but potential buyers are limited by the charging points.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, their residential estates may not have enough charging points due to existing space or electrical power output constraints.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some residents have told me that their old condominiums may have issues.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Landed property owners may also have problems and need help for their estates' power distribution to be adjusted.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: The Singapore Green Plan includes a series of initiatives to encourage a shift away from the ownership and use of internal combustion engine vehicles towards the adoption of cleaner energy vehicles, including Electric Vehicles and hybrid Electric Vehicles.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: This cleaner energy transition will almost certainly reduce air pollution and improve air quality on and around our road networks.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: It would also reduce the consumption of petrol and diesel fuels in our transport sector.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: However, the operation of Electric Vehicles still requires the production of electricity and its distribution to the expected 60,000 charging points across the island.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: As we transition to having only cleaner energy vehicles on our roads, what does that translate to in terms of the additional demands on our power production capacity, infrastructure and energy security?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: What plans are being considered for Singapore to meet these additional power demands?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: Perhaps more importantly, if Singapore were to continue to rely primarily on natural gas to generate the electricity that we need in the foreseeable future, what would the net carbon emissions savings of the transition to cleaner energy vehicles in our transport sector be?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: What steps is the Ministry considering to help us achieve this outcome?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: An energy reset is one of the five key initiatives in the Singapore Green Plan.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: Using cleaner energy has been put forward as a way to lower Singapore's carbon footprint.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: The Energy Market Authority, or EMA, announced last year that it is tapping on regional power grids for cleaner energy resources as a strategy to further diversify Singapore's energy supply.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: In assessing and refining the technical and regulatory frameworks for importing electricity into Singapore, what steps is the Ministry taking to evaluate and benchmark the carbon footprint, at source, of imported electricity to meet the cleaner energy goals of the Singapore Green Plan?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That being said, we are aware of the limitations on the land use on our island home.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our narrow tidal range and calm seas limit our ability to utilise commercial tidal and wave power.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We also do not have a river system with fast flowing water throughout the year to harness hydroelectric power.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our small physical size, high population density and land scarcity limit our potential for sustainably grown domestic biomass and large behemoth wind farms.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While ambitions to raise the capacity of solar PV capabilities six-fold by 2030 is impressive, our reliance on traditional sources of energy is still glaring.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How then can we be assured that decarbonisation will be a reality for Singapore?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: From data centres to electric transport to smart technology, all these require electricity to power.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: And as most of us are virtually spending our entire day online to work, study, learn and play, this insatiable appetite for data comes at significant environmental costs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: It is good that Singapore has been making shifts towards alternative energy sources, such as solar energy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I have asked about several Parliamentary Questions on this on the Sun Capable Project and other solar and alternative energy efforts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Can the Ministry share what other key efforts to decarbonise our electricity grid and how can our power generation companies contribute to these efforts?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The prices of natural gas are indexed to oil prices.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, electricity prices do fluctuate and Singapore is, typically, a price taker.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: But electricity prices in Singapore are generally lower now, with the opening of the energy market.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Intense competition between retailers has led to very attractive fixed price deals in contract spending over years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This brings relief for many households, with residents spending more time at home with remote working and hybrid work arrangements.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The downside to all this is that it could be challenging to encourage consumers to adopt energy-efficient measures to reduce electricity usage.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: How does the Ministry plan to meet this challenge over time?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Just recently, the Singapore Green Plan 2030 was launched and it certainly gives us plenty to look forward to, including a vision of a low carbon future where clean energy is produced, used and managed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Yet, there are some issues that we will have to consider.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: For example, in the short-term, the upfront cost of switching to cleaner machinery and vehicles would be quite hefty.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This can be challenging in the current climate where many businesses are struggling to get back on track financially.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Also, despite having no oil and gas resources of our own, Singapore is Asia's top petrochemicals hub and one of the world's top three export refining centre.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The sector and its supporting industries employ a large number of workers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Can the Ministry share which are the key trade-offs that Singapore will have to contend with?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Where are the negative impacts for industries, corporates and consumers and how will the Government help them to cope in the transition phase?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: No doubt, these developments owe something to COVID-19 but jobs affected by changes in fossil fuel demand over the longer term may eventually go beyond the refineries and include those in bunkering, rig building and other businesses in the fossil fuel industry eco-system.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Could we also consider making career conversion programmes more targeted for workers affected by this green transition through proactive pushing out of awareness campaigns and targeted ad campaigns?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Worforce Singapore has implemented career conversion programmes like the PCP but reskilling can be more proactive and should not happen only when the transition is in full swing and jobs are already being lost.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, even if the majority of our workers in potentially affected industries are able to transition successfully, I expect some will fall between the cracks into unemployment and under-employment through no fault of theirs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As has been argued by Members of this House, such as my Parliamentary colleague then, the hon Ms Sylvia Lim in the past, I urge the Government to implement measures of under-employment so that we can track this and refine our tools against bad employment outcomes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I also spoke at length about how we can push on technological and business model innovation and collaborations so that we might lead the world, including by becoming the world's most sustainable hub for specific sectors for which we have a competitive advantage such as petrochemicals and shipping, as well as pushing forward on international and regional engagement, coordination and leadership, in particular, leading a collective ASEAN 2 degree path.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Green Plan and Budget also outline other areas, including energy efficient materials and the built environment.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: To that, I also shared my optimism that given our development history in areas like engineering and process control, this time with some training and reskilling, our local workforce and can be the ones who benefit the most from this transition.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And let us put a plan against it and get ahead of the curve.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As many of my colleagues have stated, the importance of starting this in our schools to propagate the knowledge on sustainable development concepts as well as the science, in particular, material science, so that we will have an informed and empowered citizenry well before the green economy is truly upon us.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Now that we have a Singapore Green Plan 2030, we must drive our enterprises to weave in environmental, social and governance objectives.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In my maiden speech, I shared that we need to broaden our view of enterprises and entrepreneurs as having not only economic value but deep societal value at their core.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These benchmarking standards are needed so that our businesses can work towards concrete target setting.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Investors want to do more with their money and create good social outcome goals.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: An ESG mark will allow investors to make an informed decision while enterprises grow with accountability and sustainability.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Implementation of an ESG mark can benefit individual consumers and B2B clients, very much similar to International sustainable food certification, such as Marine Stewardship Council and the Rainforest Alliance.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: An ESG mark will assist one to make conscientious decisions and selecting who he or she will support and patronise.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By empowering the end consumer with more informed choice, we may drive supply chain upstream towards a greener and more impactful future.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such a mark could also assist regional and international efforts and benchmarking like how various Singapore standards have been adopted regionally.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is widely embraced and accepted in finance and investment sector as key criterion in decision-making.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It was reported that in Europe, many pensioners consciously chose asset managers with ESG capacities as their fund manager.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Much can be learned about how it has been implemented and translated into different practice models for the various industries in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I acknowledge that the ESG measurement tools are highly different for different sectors.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As such, I propose that we need to have different set of indicators that is more targeted and relevant to sectors to make it more meaningful for enterprises, investors and consumers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In addition, we need to consider the nature of smaller enterprises that their growth and development are much different even though they belong to the same sector.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, a high-end fashion chain retailer versus heartline retailer within a retail sector uses resources that are vastly different skill and rate thereby impacting our environment very differently.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, there should be a tiered ESG measurement within the same sector to ensure that we account for new ones or smaller enterprises.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must further develop our brand equity that is trusted, sustainable and impactful.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In fact, Singapore is growing as a wealth management hub.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We could establish ourselves and ensure that the impact investment capital flows through our companies creating good and impactful jobs for Singaporeans and growing our economy in a sustainable and inclusive manner.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am cognisant of the fact that setting up a ESG mark can be complex and it takes time to develop one for each sector that is well accepted by the majority of companies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is a small step that is hand signal and encourage a commitment towards sustainable and socially impactful development.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While larger companies are able to plan for this green future, SMEs might not have the resources to do so.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As the majority employer in Singapore, SMEs clearly need to play an outsized role in the green economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What are the new roles that these SMEs would play in this new economic order?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The oil and gas sector has been a fixture in Singapore's economy for more than a century.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: From having oil storage facilities in the late 1800s to the first oil refinery in the early 1960s to becoming one of the world's most important oil and chemicals hub, Singapore's fortunes have always been somewhat tied to petrochemicals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The sector continues to generate a significant portion of our GDP.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While there is no doubt that we will move to a low carbon future because of existential climate reasons, that transition is likely to be fraught with complexities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, we can simply shut the plants and go low carbon.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But there will be massive loss of jobs in the oil and gas sectors and those supporting process sector companies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We will need to work with the oil and gas companies to adopt new technologies to transit to a low carbon future.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Ministry share with us its transition plan that balances our ambitions with support for our workers and economies?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Second, it is not only just the oil and gas sector that faces intricate complexities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are many other companies and their workers who depend on petrochemicals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, the logistics sector depend on an extensive fleet of delivery vehicles.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The infrastructure and technology for them to transit to electric vehicles is still nascent.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The future seems to be one where we seek to reduce carbon footprint progressively.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Ministry share how we can help these companies with the transition?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Even so, there can also be opportunities within the low-carbon space.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: New industries and research outfits might be set up or evolved to provide new investments and jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Ministry share what are these new jobs and industries that will be created?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can we better prepare our Singaporeans to take up such opportunities?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: My response was this: "If for any reasons, our petrochemical companies exit Singapore, it is quite likely that they move to a different location with even less robust carbon emission standards to minimise costs.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We have been continually shoring up our coastal areas, especially those which were reclaimed not so long ago.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Increasingly we are feeling the impact of rising sea waters.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: During the 2019 National Day Rally (NDR), Prime Minister presented the long-term plan of coastal protection against rising sea levels.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: He mentioned that from the city to our east coast areas are low-lying grounds that will be vulnerable to flooding when sea level rises.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: One of the exciting projects he mentioned was the building of polders following the example of the Netherlands along the coastline.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: These are seawalls built further out at sea and the water is then pumped out.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It will create new land that could be used for housing and other purposes.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This is to reclaim a series of islands offshore, from Marina East all the way to Changi, then join them up with barrages and create a huge freshwater reservoir similar to Marina Reservoir.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In this way, we can further enhance our water resilience.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Last year alone, the Government spent $100 billion in four Budgets.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Since the projects will yield huge benefits for our country in the long term, can we consider bringing in these large infrastructure projects forward so we can realise the benefits even earlier?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It also helps to promote and build our SMEs in their capabilities as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Building polders and creating new land that can also be sold and raise funds for the project.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Given our finite land and sea space, how will the building of the polders and offshore islands affect our shipping lanes?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Will our Navy have any more waters to sail after the construction?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on this very exciting project, with what has been done since 2019?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And I would like to ask the Minister whether can he share with the House how does our Government ensure that coastal adaptation measures are cost-effective and adequately resourced, given this is a long-term and large-scale effort?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
