text: Like what our Prime Minister said during the NDR 2019, we must make this effort now.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Otherwise, one day, our children and grandchildren will be ashamed of what our generation did not do.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our blue spaces are precious and debris pollution, coastal development and high usage of these spaces can have lasting negative impact on our marine environment.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When we factor in climate change and the fact that only about 30% of our island is only less than five metres above the mean sea level, I believe that coastal protection needs to be a priority for now and for future generations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can the Minister update on PUB's effort, since assuming this role, and what are the future plans?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And will there be a coastal protection masterplan similar to the Green Building masterplan?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With climate change, we can expect such extreme weather events to become more common.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As we continue to convert more of our forests into developments, we lose the many protective benefits of forests in moderating the impacts of extreme weather.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, forests help slow the flow of water into our drainage system, reducing flooding risks.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Therefore, when floods happen, we cannot point the finger solely at climate change, when we ourselves have been partly to blame.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As we cut down more forests, we will have to spend more on ensuring that our physical drainage infrastructure and flood response systems can keep up.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the Ministry has an established monitoring and response system for flooding, what are the plans to address the root causes of flooding in vulnerable areas?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the Ministry's flood protection plans adequately account for possible future increases in extreme rainfall?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Beyond flash floods causing destruction and inconveniences, the incessant rainfall had also resulted in the uprooting of trees, posing safety concerns for Singaporeans.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Thus, it is pivotal that we have a comprehensive and coordinated understanding on Singapore's level of flood resilience.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: One, improvements in existing drainage systems and buildings in low-lying areas.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Many of these flash floods occur in low-lying areas with some in private estates.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Unlike the public housing, the private estates do not have a dedicated Town Council to handle and address these municipal issues.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Would any support be provided to enhance the infrastructure on drainage system in existing private estates and older buildings?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Two, periodic assessments of efficacy of measures to allow for nimble, adaptive changes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: From the findings, are there more areas that need to be further reviewed and what would the periodic assessment on the efficacy of the measures entail?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While extensive measures have been adopted to protect our coastal areas and reduce and flood risks, however, with the best of efforts, we are always vulnerable to the forces of nature.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I suggest we increase the vegetation topsoil to serve as absorbent layer for water drainage especially in areas like park connectors along the water banks or planting along the roads.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, please take your three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With climate change, comes more extreme weather conditions.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore is no exception and we are experiencing more unpredictable and intense rainfalls.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Going forward, we can continue to expect more of such sudden and heavy precipitation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are some of PUB's plans to mitigate inland floods in the face of this challenge?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we continue to develop and become more densely built up, how can we ensure that we have enough green lungs and basins to absorb the surface run-off?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Do our reservoirs and catchment tanks have sufficient capacities?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What upgrading and assistance measures have we implemented to protect and help residences and shophouse in older, low-lying areas?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry provide an update on the safety measures, such as higher barricades for pavements next to drains, for the protection of pedestrians during floods?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Temperatures have been rising in Singapore, and our residents have been feeling it outdoors and in their homes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are some measures that we, as individuals, can take to help reduce heat emissions.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Air-con cools an interior by releasing the waste heat to the outside.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Adjusting the air-con to a comfortable temperature of around or just above 25 degree Celsius instead of blasting colder air, will help reduce the amount of heat that it generates to the exterior.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The use of refrigeration has a similar impact on external temperatures.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Reducing our demand for non-essential cold items, for example, drinks, ice-cream and desserts, is another way to help reduce heat emissions.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry advise what more can we do to reduce heat emissions from human activities?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Increasingly, due to human activities, such as transportation and intense use of air-conditioning, Singapore is experiencing worsening Urban Heat Island effect, in short it is called UHI.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is generally understood to describe the air temperature difference between urban and rural areas.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, in the Singapore context, it would mean the difference between our built-up and green areas.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How does the Government measure the extent of the UHI effect and has any research been conducted?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Which sectors are the main contributors to the urban heat island effect in Singapore and what has the Government done to mitigate or reduce it?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Does the Ministry have any new measures to reduce this and how can we, as individuals, contribute to this effort?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Louis Ng, please take your four cuts together.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As I mentioned during the climate change Motion, Singaporeans increasingly live their lives in a sustainable way.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They should be given more information with which to make their consumption decisions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The UK already requires all big companies to include emissions data in their annual reports, and the EU provides large amounts of emissions data on all facilities level across its member states.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government has shared that company-level emissions may reveal confidential business performance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this case, I propose that we publish a ranking of the top emitters without sharing their exact emissions level.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This allows the public to make more informed consumption decisions without compromising the business confidentiality of our businesses.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It strikes a fair balance between the trade-offs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This astounding amount of e-waste will only increase.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If not handled properly, e-waste contains small amounts of harmful substances that can threaten our health and our environment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can MSE share whether we are on track to meet this target?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can MSE also share its plans on how it will raise awareness on the EPR and make recycling e-waste convenient for all, so that we can all do our part to make the EPR a success?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Last year, I shared with the House about the Zero Waste Masterplan in Nee Soon East.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I talked about how we had saved 39,792 disposables since the launch of our Zero Waste Masterplan in April 2019.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: COVID-19, unfortunately, threw a spanner in the works but we will restart the Zero Waste Masterplan once we can.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I commend MSE for putting together a diverse Citizens' Workgroup to tackle this issue of excessive consumption of disposables.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How will MSE incorporate the recommendations from the recently concluded Citizens' Workgroup into its plans to better manage disposables in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the public service take the lead by committing to end the use of all disposables at all public service events?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Ministry also announced that it will put in place a Deposit Refund Scheme for beverage containers by 2022 as the first phase of the EPR framework for packaging waste, including plastics.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the MSE share more details on the progress on this?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, food waste is one of the biggest sources of waste in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am currently working on a Private Member’s Bill to tackle food waste and hope to introduce a Good Samaritan's Food Donation Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have completed our first round of consultations and I am glad to have the strong support from civil society and industry players.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am also glad to see the Government taking active steps to address food waste.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MSE announced that it will introduce mandatory food waste segregation requirements for large commercial and industrial premises.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond segregation, it is also important for companies to be aware of the amount of food waste they dispose of.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Data about food waste generated will help companies better manage their processes to reduce waste.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is both a win for sustainability and for the companies’ bottom lines.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will MSE consider requiring companies that have to segregate food waste for treatment to also report the amount of food waste segregated?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In the Green Plan, one of the key pillars is sustainable living, where policies will be geared towards propelling us into a zero-waste nation powered by a circular economy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To tackle our plastics waste issue, we will, therefore, also need a reduction of plastics consumption, especially single-use plastics.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: When we are just focusing solely on recycling, this neglect on reducing our waste is what drives production which, in turn, creates carbon footprint.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I understand that the citizens' workgroup on reducing excessive consumption of disposables was convened and it called for a fee for each plastic bag if they take three or more of them at supermarkets.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I wish to lend my support to this call and ask that the Ministry also study a single-use plastics charge across retailers and F&B outlets, phased in over five years, to encourage a reduction in plastics waste and look for alternatives.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Concerns raised on the potential negative effects on lower income households can be tackled by having a rebate scheme.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The authorities can also work with charity groups and non-profit organisations to give out complimentary reusable bags.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I repeat my call in my Budget debate speech last year for mindsets to shift in the way we consume, to only use what we need to use.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In supermarkets or shops, can we use more of good quality reusable shopping bags like this one, something that I have been using for the last nearly 20 years?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If we only need to use, say, one or two plastic bags for refuse disposal a day, can we not take more plastic bags than we need?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In this way, we may end up using fewer plastic bags and may still have enough bags for our refuse.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The grant seeks to raise the hygiene and cleaning standards of public toilets.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A corollary aim of the TIP is to encourage the removal of smoking corners.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In designing the grant parameters, what impact does NEA foresee in the event of the removal of smoking corners from hawker centres with existing smoking corners?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Specifically, what is the assessment of the displacement effect of smokers from hawker centres out into the community?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While I appreciate NEA and the medical advice would lean on the very reasonable hope that some smokers would quit the habit as a result of the removal of smoking corners, there is a greater likelihood, at least in the immediate term, of smokers migrating from hawker centres to other areas in the community.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This includes smoking in the comfort of their own homes, potentially leading to more nuisance complaints from their fellow neighbours.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, what is the policy connection between toilet upgrading and the removal of smoking corners?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Quite simply, the TIP grant and its objectives, while independently commendable, will create the prospect of new disamenities in other Town Council-managed areas and, possibly, between HDB flat dwellers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Town Councils may well have to create new smoking areas somewhere else close to the hawker centres shortly after the grant is given to the Town Council, or even reinstate a smoking corner in the market after the grant has been disbursed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would it not be a better policy for NEA to tie the TIP grant with specific compulsory criteria related to the renovation of toilets that are energy-saving, green and come with lower life-cycle costs, in line with the Government's Green Plan and targets?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, some of the recommended features in the TIP include the toilet feedback management system – something I believe is akin to those found in shopping centres and/or the airport where users rate toilet cleanliness.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Other additions NEA has recommended include the installation of toilet pedestal mounted bidets.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is open to question whether some of these recommended features under the TIP are practical in the long term.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is difficult to imagine how much care must be taken by a cleaner to hygienically clean a toilet pedestal mounted bidet and, separately, how easily such a feature can be damaged in a heavy-use setting.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would be important to study the steady state condition of the pilot toilet at this hawker centre, which should be perceptible after a few months of use, allowing for a better perspective on the effectiveness of the measures proposed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With hawker culture recently added to the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, it would be important to get this done right so that a broadly consistent toilet hygiene standard is consistent across all hawker centres in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, the TIP also envisages an enhanced maintenance regime, the details of which have not been communicated to Town Councils.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Does NEA envision an increase in manpower to achieve the cleanliness standards required?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And in light of the tiered nature of the grant, how many hawker centres in Singapore currrently do not have smoking areas and, out of these, how many are newly constructed hawker centres and how many are legacy hawker centres?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Through various agencies, including NTUC, the Ministry is working with them to support SMEs to build up their capabilities, carry out our product development and carry out job redesigning and so forth.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: I hope that the Ministry can speed up this particular programme and put more resources into it.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The outbreak of COVID-19 has put even more demands on this industry now as public hygiene and cleanliness come into the spotlight.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Almost overnight, to control the spread of the pandemic, the use of face masks, gloves, plastics and various containers used for food deliveries has become an environmental nightmare.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The indiscriminate disposal of face masks and gloves, especially if not properly done so, could choke up our waterways and pose a hazard to our environment.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The situation was exacerbated during the circuit breaker period when many of the foreign workers in this particular sector could not work.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Water got clogged in the drains, open parks and, in many areas, grass was not cut, mosquito breeding and outbreaks of dengue clusters became another hazard.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Then there is the volume of waste coming from medical centres, hospitals which needs to be addressed, ranging from syringes, face masks to disposable personal protective equipment.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Are the existing waste facilities able to cope with this unusual volume of medical waste?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: As the COVID-19 period prolongs, may I also ask what is the Ministry’s plan to support and help the industry to transform so that they are able to better cope with the new challenges they face in this particular sector?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Sadly, I do not see much improvement in the state of cleanliness in the estate.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: My grassroots leaders and I still see cigarette butts, empty cigarette packets, drink bottles, plastic bottles, plastic bags, used tissues, used face masks thrown all over the floor.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: At hawker centres, you will see chopstick wrappers strewn all over the ground as well.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Despite the increased number of summonses issued against litterbugs, I feel that the littering situation has not improved in the past five years?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: NEA must send a message to all litterbugs that their acts of littering have negatively affected the environment and that the litter must be picked up by others.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Hopefully, with a Corrective Work Order stint, the offender will see the mess caused by their own actions and acknowledge their role to keep the environment clean.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Why should the average Singapore citizen have to live with a dirty environment caused by a few inconsiderate litterbugs?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: My first cut relates to fostering individual ownership for a clean Singapore.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Good personal and public hygiene are our first two lines of defence against diseases.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Over the years, the Ministry has rolled out different initiatives to raise cleanliness and hygiene standards in public spaces and promote positive social norms, such as the SG Clean Quality Mark.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Sustained collective action will be imperative to inculcate a sense of personal and social responsibility in the community.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Could a Ministry share more on its efforts and progress of the various initiatives to soster individual and social responsibility?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: My second cut relates to the transformation of our Environmental Services industry, specifically Pest Management.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The Pest Management industry plays a critical role in securing premises against vectors and vector-borne diseases in Singapore and in safeguarding our public health.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In 2019, the Ministry announced that the Pest Management sector will be integrated with the Environmental Services Industry Transformation Map.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Many regard this to be timely as this will also accord opportunities for our local enterprises and provide meaningful jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: My third cut relates to sustaining the hawker culture.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Many of us celebrated when our hawker culture was recognised by UNESCO in December 2020.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Seven centres have been completed and the remainder 13 are to follow.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We understand that the key reason we engage operators through the Socially-conscious Enterprise Hawker Centre (SEHC) model was to leverage their private sector experience so as to better improve the management of hawker centres and meet our community needs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The initial implementation saw resistance from hawkers due to higher cost and inflexible contract conditions that had to be worked out.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Since then, the Government has announced that the remaining 13 centres will be run under the SEHC model.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: How will NEA continue to work with social enterprise operators to ensure that the success of these new hawker centres while also factoring in the earlier feedback from hawkers relating to the challenges they face under the SEHC model?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, to protect and preserve the heritage and traditions of our hawker culture in an authentic manner is challenging.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hawker centres were built rapidly throughout the 1970s and early 1980s to resettle the street hawkers and to cater for the demand of the population in the new satellite towns, but they have actually been declining in popularity since the late 1980s as Singaporeans looked for a better eating environment.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As our F&B scene become more sophisticated and diverse but also more expensive, hawker centres remain a source of good, affordable meals for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, high rentals and running costs have caught up making it very difficult for new hawkers to enter the market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even allowing some hawker centres to be run by social enterprises did not solve the high running cost problem.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the most pressing problem of the hawker trade is to replace an entire generation of retiring hawkers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many of them do not have successors because their children mostly do not want to take over the back-breaking trade and it is also their wish not to have their children taking over from them.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is also the inherent clash between providing affordable meals which means that the hawker trade will be of low profitability and attracting young Singaporeans into the industry.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, there may be a need to review the policy of positioning our hawker food as a source of cheap meals.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Perhaps our focus should be on the preservation of our food culture and recipes, much like the intellectual property in other industries, whilst allowing the form of the hawker centre to evolve in tandem with society.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I made the call to introduce this scheme in 2016.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I am repeating my call today as within the last four years, I have met a number of needy residents, a couple of them are ex-offenders, who shared that they have culinary skills and expressed their aspiration to run hawker stall with an affordable operating cost.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The hardship scheme may not be a standalone scheme.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It could be a sub-scheme under the Incubation Stall Programme or ISP, specifically targeting two groups – needy Singaporeans and ex-offenders which are specifically beneficiaries of ComCare scheme and Yellow Ribbon Project.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I suggest that the scheme be re-introduced and to implemented as a Socially-conscious Enterprise Hawker Centre (SEHC) model which would be congruous with its social mission, a point which Senior of State Dr Amy Khor has alluded to before in this House.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Providing such opportunity and support to needy individuals and ex-offenders, among us, via the hardship scheme for hawker centre stall is, indeed, a very noble social mission.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, please take your three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our efforts to honour our hawker trade had culminated in the successful inscription of our Hawker Culture on the UNESCO List of Intangible Cultural Heritage.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must continue to support and sustain the hawker trade so that it will prosper for many more generations to come.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How would the Government identify these hawkers, and what will be done to support both the retiring and aspiring hawkers during these transitions?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our hawker centres are our national canteens and provide a wide range of affordable and delicious food.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are highly desired in neighbourhoods and many residents in the newer estates request for them.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has disrupted our everyday lives significantly, including our construction sector.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many building projects had to be postponed and works are being delayed.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of the most important qualities of a civilised society is public hygiene.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Each one of us need to step up to keep our environment clean.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Over the years, the Government had conducted several campaigns to encourage individuals to do their part.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The encouragement include keeping premises clean and pest-free, refraining from littering, keeping toilets clean and dry and so on.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I agree with many concerned citizens that we need collective action to achieve our vision of a clean Singapore, instead of a "cleaned Singapore" relying on an army of cleaners to pick up after us.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should aim for high cleanliness standards even after the pandemic is over.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In what other ways and through which channels would the Ministry tap on to continue to encourage socially desirable behaviours, and foster individual and social responsibility?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin, please take your four cuts together.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The recent recognition of Singapore's Hawker culture as an intangible cultural heritage under UNESCO and the COVID-19 pandemic has taught us many lessons about our wet markets and hawker centres.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Wet markets are such an important part of our culture and I recently had the opportunity to interact with two young women Pam and Tahira, who initiated the Pass the Pasar Movement to encourage more Singaporeans to visit our wet markets and share the experiences.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such efforts continue to make these precious spaces relevant for the next generation and, as someone from the younger generation I disagree that hawker centres are less popular among my generation today as many of us "tabao"-ed these places during the circuit breaker.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Government be considering further enhancements to the infrastructure of our hawker centres to ensure they will: firstly, be safe and clean; and secondly, continue to be relevant and exciting for our people from all walks of life.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we embark on our sustainability push, will the Government also be looking into how to make hawker centres and wet markets more sustainable in the long run and reduce food wastage at scale?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: COVID-19 has shown that food security is of utmost importance.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: During critical periods when supply chains could be disrupted, the delivery of vital goods could be impaired and in Singapore we are investing in increasing local food production as a safeguard.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will the Government ensure that the new support schemes meet painpoints and are effective in helping our farmers to grow the local agri-food sector capabilities?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can we also have the Government's assurance that the boost in locally produced food will go first and foremost towards meeting domestic consumption, or if they are grown for export, will that count towards our "30 by 30" target?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Achieving our aquaculture goals should be done in a sustainable and resource efficient manner that is friendly to our marine environment.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some of our sea-based farms are located near community spaces.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, near Bendera Bay in the Southern Islands.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For such farms in close proximity to our blue spaces, I hope we are extra mindful of the potential impact.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Could the Government elaborate how close containment sea-based farming systems are more energy efficient and environmentally friendly than traditional sea-based farming systems?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Does the Government have additional plans to increase the resilience of the aquaculture sector?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And does the Government plan to have support for the labour market to adjust to these new technologies?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It has been more than a year since the formation of SFA.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How has the consolidation of food functions into a single agency benefited the industry?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we evolve into a new norm, food delivery services have also played an important role over the past year with more people handling food before it reaches the consumer.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond consumers indicating how many stars out of five on food delivery platforms, can we indicate cleanliness and hygiene, for example, and will delivery riders be equipped and trained to better handle food?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Given the potential impact on livelihoods and the environment, how had the relevant stakeholders been involved in the masterplanning process?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will these experienced farmers and their staff be invited to participate in the new plans and be given assistance to change or upgrade their operations so that they can be part of the new production initiatives?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For those who choose to retire or discontinue, what assistance or compensation will be provided for them?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will there be any disruptions to our food production during this transition period.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, I declare my interest as the Council Member of the Institute of Singapore Chartered Accountants and I am working with a Singaporean bank.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For a new eco-system to flourish, availability of financing is important.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will the Ministry consider working with MAS and Association of Banks of Singapore to develop Singapore into a global, if not a regional green trade financing hub.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, concepts like sustainable financing and carbon credits are still relatively new to many local companies which are unsure of the accounting treatment.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Thus, I also urge the Ministry to work with the Accountancy body or Singapore Accountancy Commission to formulate a prescriptive set of accounting standards and framework.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am confident we can be the credible accountancy and financing hub for sustainability.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The scenes of panic buying at the supermarkets are still fresh in our mind from last year.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: As an island state, while we are ranked as number one in the EIU Global Food Security Index against countries like US, Switzerland, Norway and Germany.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: But this does not give us comfort when you start to read about countries shutting down their borders, sea and airports and also thousands of workers, farmers and truckers stricken by the virus.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We were able to draw on our stockpile each time the shelves were emptied.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We were able to ensure not only food but medical and petrol supply were flowing and essential services were not disrupted, giving assurances to the population.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Now that the pandemic has gone global, I am sure many countries who did not do their maths would be scrambling to get their supplies of essential food stuff and others.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The market would be more competitive for everyone.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Disruption in supply can not only be caused by a global pandemic.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Today, we live in an age of increasing uncertainty.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We have in recent years seen unforeseeable disasters, some man-made and others natural.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: For example, wars, terrorist attacks, earthquakes, tsunamis, epidemics and nuclear reactor accidents, and even climate change resulting in crop failure or destruction of farmland due to wild fires.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Maybe we should aim to get Temasek and our other local enterprises to increase their overseas investments in food production, in food supply so that we can further enhance our food security together with our neighbours.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Are we building up a pool of talents in the field of agriculture technology?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Increasingly, with the growing demand for meat substitutes, we will see more novel foods for sale, such as plant-based proteins, cultured or lab-grown meat and edible farmed insects.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Without the history of safe use, how can we ensure that new food production technologies, such as lab-grown meat, are safe for our consumers?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: In the past, we had referred to the guidelines and the experience of other nations with bigger populations.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: As a pioneer, we do not have such data on human consumption to depend on.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This consumption rate will likely double in 2060.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Taking into consideration that water treatment technologies can be energy intensive, what are PUB's targets to improve its energy efficiency of water treatment?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: What is the progress of that project and how many other reservoirs will be similarly equipped with floating solar panels?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In 2018, PUB and NEA announced that Tuas Nexus will be first in Singapore to treat both used water and food waste in the same facility to generate bio-gas for electricity production.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Are there more plans to develop similar facilities to enhance sustainability?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I hope the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment would shed light on these queries.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We are collecting every drop of water and recycling it where possible.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some of it is purified into NEWater, one of our four national taps and recycled into our water supply.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is made possible with PUB's robust network of tunnels and sewers, including the Deep Tunnel Sewerage System, which funnels used water from households and industries to our water reclamation plants for treatment.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This water is then further treated into NEWater in the NEWater factories.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I will talk about three areas in enhancing our water resources.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Used water is a precious resource that must be protected.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some companies irresponsibly discharge toxic waste and prohibited substances into our sewers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This could potentially disrupt the water reclamation process, and even compromise our NEWater supply.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What are the Ministry's plans to deter such harmful and dangerous practices?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will there be more surveillance and harsher deterrent measures to protect our water supply?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, we need to improve our water efficiency.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Singapore's success in re-using water is borne out of necessity, as we have very limited water resources.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We cannot rest on our laurels, as we face significant challenges ahead.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Most of this demand will be driven by non-domestic use.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many older buildings which have older fittings, they are less efficient in using water compared to the newer systems.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Older toilets also use more water when flushing, compared to newer and more water-efficient systems.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This can contribute to higher water consumption, particularly in the buildings with higher human traffic, like shopping malls and offices.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What plans does the Ministry have in place to manage the increasing water demand and improve water efficiency?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is insufficient to rely on regulations alone to manage water demand.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Every individual, household and organisation in Singapore must make an effort to manage their water consumption and reduce usage where possible.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Educating the public and businesses on water use can help to identify abnormal water usage and encourage the adoption of water-saving habits.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some of my residents informed me that while they would like to reduce their water usage, they are unable to identify which activities consume the most water from the monthly data in their bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some even come to my Meet-the-People sessions to enquire about this and about their water bills.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the PUB provide updates about the new technologies to monitor and improve the efficiency of water use?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Ageing waterpipes, corrosion and changing soil conditions can lead to pipe leakages.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: When pipes leak, precious water is lost and wasted from the system.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: There have been cases of large leaks or pipe bursts where a huge volume of water shoots out from the ground.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Water supply is thus disrupted in some cases, causing inconvenience to some residents and businesses.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As most of the pipelines are underground, small leaks can go unnoticed and may eventually develop to bigger leaks.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: What are the steps by PUB to manage these pipelines and whether they are new technologies that can be adopted to better detect and prevent leaks?

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In 2020, the world had to battle record-breaking forest fires, the most active Atlantic hurricane season on record until they ran out of alphabets to name the hurricanes, more frequent floods and droughts and other weather events leading to large-scale devastation.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As a low-lying island, Singapore remains fundamentally vulnerable to the impact of climate change, which poses an existential threat to us.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We take a considered, committed and collective approach to the global climate crisis.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: My colleagues from five Ministries which are taking key measures for climate action in our Green Plan, are collectively responding to the points that Members have raised during this Budget debate and Committee of Supply and presenting the comprehensive action we are taking to put words into action to fight climate change.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I chair the Inter-Ministerial Committee on Climate Change which was established in 2007 to coordinate a whole-of-nation response.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: While we respond as individual Ministries, we have a collective thought out action plan behind this.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: First, to formulate and execute our national plans to prepare ourselves for the impact of climate change.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Second, to ensure that Singapore contributes to global climate action.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We made these commitments, well aware that they are challenging, given our national circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We will continue to review our climate goals with the aim of achieving net zero emissions as soon as viable.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Allow me, Mdm Chairman, to take a step back to explain the thinking and guiding principles behind how we approach this global crisis.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: For a small island city-state like Singapore, climate change poses an asymmetrical challenge.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: While Singapore contributes around 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, the totality of global emissions, 100%, including the other 99.9%, affects us too and often, more seriously than it affects larger better endowed countries.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: So, we must do our best to tackle climate change, but ultimately, we depend on a collective global effort to address the issue at a global level.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked about what Singapore is doing to promote this global collaboration.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Singapore has been working hard to strengthen consensus and galvanise climate action regionally and globally.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This has been especially critical at a time when the multilateral system is under strain from protectionism and unilateral action, further exacerbated by the challenges of COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Singapore is often called upon, as a knowledgeable, fair and honest broker, to facilitate discussions to forge consensus for the work under the UNFCCC and its implementation rules.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Unfortunately, COP-26 did not take place in Glasgow last year due to COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But our officials have continued to work actively on important international issues, such as rules for carbon markets and more stringent reporting of national emissions and climate action.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We are also actively shaping multilateral discussions on reducing international transportation emissions, as suggested by Ms Mariam Jaafar.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: At the same time, we have been carefully planning and implementing, in an integrated and coordinated long-term manner, the measures we need to take domestically for a low carbon future.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As a small country with limited alternative energy sources, land and manpower, our trade-offs are much starker than what most countries face.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Our carbon emissions set real cross-cutting constraints on our development and the daily lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We need to find ways to break out of these constraints through careful long-term planning and innovations in policy and technology.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We look for synergies to give ourselves the space to grow, but when it is needed, we also have to make well-considered, real trade-offs.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Miss Rachel Ong, Ms Yeo Wan Ling and Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked about these trade-offs and how we are pursuing decarbonisation despite our constraints.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Singapore is both a city and a country.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Within our small land space, we need to accommodate not just housing, parks and commercial centres, but also power plants, reservoirs, air- and sea- ports, and industries.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The trade-offs are real, and often the choices are difficult.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: For example, unlike bigger countries, we do not have large plots of land for extensive solar farms.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: There are many competing land users, as we have debated in this House over these last few weeks.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But we do strive to maximise solar energy by aggressively deploying panels on the rooftops of suitable HDB blocks.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: My colleague, the Minister for National Development will update us on this later.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: To supplement our limited land, we are also using our reservoirs for floating solar farms, something which several Members asked about.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This allows us to use our reservoirs not just for water but also for solar power and to provide green lungs for recreation and water activities as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Second, securing our water and food supply is a key national priority.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: When I hear Members speak about recycling, do not forget that water recycling is recycling too, and we are one of the leaders in the world in water recycling.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And when we count water recycling, our recycling rate is really very high.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We are making a major push for food security as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Heng announced the new Agri-Food Cluster Transformation Fund for technology adoption in our agri-food sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We actively engage A*STAR and our Institutes of Higher Learning to develop novel, resource efficient approaches for food and water.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: These will help us break out of our constraints to secure our food, through careful long-term planning and innovations in policy and technology, and keep costs affordable while minimising carbon emissions.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In that one long sentence, we can see the dilemmas and the trade-offs that we have to make in each one of the steps that we take.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Since the time Mr Lee Kuan Yew called for us to create a metropolis out of mudflats, we have always balanced development, conservation and the environment.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This is reflected in Singapore being among the best 20 countries in the world today in terms of Emissions Intensity (EI), that is, emissions per GDP dollar.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We have been able to grow our economy, create jobs, while keeping our emissions per GDP dollar one of the lowest in the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And this is in spite of all of our constraints.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I listened very carefully to the speeches made by all the Members, but was particularly struck by the thoughtful analyses made by Ms Mariam Jaafar and Prof Koh Lian Pin.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They have deep knowledge of these areas and they understand well the trade-offs as Singapore seeks new ways to grow our economy within a carbon-constrained envelope, and how we can balance conservation, development and jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They have made several good suggestions and useful proposals which we will certainly study very closely.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Our workers have to shift to jobs in new areas of growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: One example is the energy and chemicals sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Abdul Samad, who is with us in this House, will be well aware of this.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: He and his unions are doing the actual work – they are doing the work helping workers to cope with this challenge and make the transition.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The switch to cleaner energy will reduce demand for more carbon-intensive fossil fuels.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: However, demand for sustainable fuels and higher value-added petrochemical products and specialty chemicals will grow.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The modern green eco-system needs such products, such as in solar panels, batteries, thermal insulation for buildings, durable and light-weight parts for electric vehicles.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And we are investing in sustainable energy too.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Neste, the world’s largest producer of renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel, is expanding its production capacity here.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They are already here, and they are expanding their production.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: When completed, Singapore will be home to Neste’s largest renewable products plant, creating new jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Many of the major energy and chemical companies in Singapore have also committed to reach net zero by 2050 and Singapore will partner them in this shift.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The public sector will lead by example, by embarking on a comprehensive whole-of-Government programme, called GreenGov.SG, to reduce our resource footprint and carbon emissions, and to enable the rest of the economy to do likewise.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment will speak more about this later.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Sharael Taha asked about our plans for carbon tax and the resulting impact.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Heng said in his Budget speech, the Government will be reviewing the trajectory and level of the carbon tax, post-2023, in consultation with industry and expert groups.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We seek a carbon tax level that will incentivise companies and consumers to switch to carbon friendly products, services and activities, while promoting industry innovation and new green growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: There are already significant new investments in sustainable industries in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Hyundai is constructing a research and development centre and electric vehicle pilot production facility in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: These examples illustrate how Singapore can leverage and is leveraging our strengths in R&D, advanced manufacturing and logistics to create more opportunities and good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In addition, we are taking steps to establish Singapore as a centre for carbon credits trading and services, for sustainability consultancy, and to play a significant role in green finance for sustainable development in a growing Asia.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In fact, we are calling on Prof Koh Lian Pin on his expertise to help us develop in this area.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This will also create new high quality jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We are similarly taking a proactive approach to protect ourselves from the effects of climate change.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This requires forward planning as climate change threats require solutions that span many decades.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We have not been sitting on our hands.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Taking early action will often cost less in the long run, than trying to raise land levels or put in protection later.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Minister for Sustainability and the Environment will be elaborating on our plans.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Being prepared for the future also includes developing new sustainability solutions, not just for ourselves but also for the rest of the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: R&D plans in our USS domain include enhancing our resilience in energy, water and food, and developing more cost-effective solutions to reduce our greenhouse gas emissions.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We will also increase our R&D efforts in the use of renewables and emerging low-carbon technologies such as hydrogen and carbon capture, utilisation and storage, a subject which Miss Cheryl Chan is very knowledgeable about and spoke very lucidly on.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We will also develop solutions against rising sea levels, urban heat island effects, and other challenges brought about by climate change.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As a “living lab”, we will continue to serve as a test-bed for innovative solutions that can be exported globally in cities around the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But most important of all, we need to overcome this existential challenge together, as a whole-of-nation.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Ms Hany Soh asked how the Government intends to achieve this whole-of-nation effort.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Green Plan reflects this Government’s aspirations and commitment towards sustainable development for us.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Many Singaporeans, especially young Singaporeans, are motivated and energised by this vision and want to play an active role.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And our desire is to partner every Singaporean to transform Singapore into a glowing global city of sustainability.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: My colleagues from the respective Ministries will be elaborating on the initiatives under the Green Plan and responding to the specific comments from Members.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Our enhanced NDC, LEDS, and Green Plan have set challenging and ambitious goals for Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I am confident that by rallying together as one, we will rise to the challenge, re-invent Singapore and create a brighter and sustainable future for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: So, with your permission, may I put on record our recognition for all the engineers out there.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Climate change is one of the gravest threats facing mankind and Singapore.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: What is at stake is the survival and future of our small island state.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: One or two more degrees Celsius increase may not sound like much but if sea level rises a few metres, our sunny island could literally be in the sea.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Climate change could also threaten our food and water supply.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We have to take climate change seriously, study its impact and start preparing ourselves now.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We have to develop a long-term climate action plan to both mitigate and adapt to climate change.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Everything else must bend at the knee to safeguard the existence of our island nation.” We must take climate change seriously.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The Government is fully committed to take decisive action to mitigate climate change and adapt to its impact.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I was most encouraged by the passion and concerns shown.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: But our efforts alone will not turn the tide.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Climate action requires urgent, collective and coordinated efforts by all countries, big and small.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We have been working actively within ASEAN and the broader international community to deliver a global response to climate change and contribute to the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Just as the invention of the steam engine and discovery of fossil fuels propelled us into the industrial age, the energy transition from fossil fuel to renewable energy will redefine how we power the global economy.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This revolution will be driven by policy makers, consumers, inventors and investors who recognise the opportunities that will arise from a circular, low carbon economy.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We must catch and ride this new global wave of sustainability.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Many MNCs are putting Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) considerations at the core of their business and investment decisions.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Since Independence, instead of pursuing growth at all costs, we have insisted on quality, inclusive and sustainable growth.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Each generation of Singaporeans must see ourselves as stewards of our nation.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We must pass on a better Singapore to the generations of Singaporeans that will come after us, just as the previous generations had done for us.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We must build on our past achievements, strive to overcome our present limitations and pioneer new solutions for a more sustainable future.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Getting to that future will be a whole-of-nation effort, requiring every Government agency, individual, business, research institution, community group and civil society organisation to work in unison.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Sustainability is not an isolated programme or initiative but about engineering a whole system and cultivating a new way of life.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Each challenge and its associated solution will impact on another.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It is a commitment of this PAP Government to our present and future generations, to chart a common vision for a sustainable future and a roadmap for everyone.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Through the Green Plan, sustainability will shape our economy, our infrastructure, our way of life.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It will fundamentally change how we live, work and play.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The Government will set the broad policy direction and the public sector will lead the change.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Through the GreenGov.SG initiative, it will exemplify sustainability in its actions and lead market demand for sustainable products and services.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: More importantly, we want the Green Plan to spark a national conversation and energise Singaporeans to take action.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Every Singaporean must be involved in this transformation because, first, sustainability is not costless.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Just as we pay for our security and social services, we will have to pay a bit more for greener goods and services, adjust to less convenience in our daily lives, or reskill for green jobs in new industries.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We cannot incur these costs without a national consensus.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Second, while climate change may feel abstract for individuals, it is our individual actions that determine the collective outcome.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: If we avoid disposables, buy locally produced food and prefer energy-efficient appliances, greener and more sustainable business models will emerge.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Third, we are excited about the new business opportunities that the sustainability sector can bring that will benefit Singaporeans and Singapore.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The Green Plan will also contribute to the international sustainability agenda and global climate goals.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The Green Plan will lay out our priorities for collaboration with our international stakeholders.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It is in our interest, and that of the world, to catalyse the development of green solutions, such as green hydrogen, and carbon capture, utilisation and storage.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We are well placed to contribute to the global effort.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As a living lab, where new solutions can be test-bedded and exported to the region and beyond.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And as a financial hub and talent hub, where green capital can find common objectives with skilled entrepreneurs and workers.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This will allow us to pace our green transition correctly and stay in sync with the global trajectory so that we do not move too hastily and hurt our economic competitiveness and the livelihoods of Singaporeans, or move too slowly and get left behind.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Some have asked if the Green Plan is just a compilation of existing initiatives.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The Green Plan is a long-term and living plan that will evolve as we go along.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will update our targets and strategies as new technologies and practicable solutions avail themselves.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The Green Plan is also not just an MSE or even a Government plan, but a blueprint that we have set out for ourselves as a nation and therefore, we have six other Ministers speaking on it.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Everyone must work together to achieve our vision.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: While some targets are existing, new and enhanced targets have been included.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Even in areas where targets remain the same, we are putting in place comprehensive and concrete near-to-medium term plans to achieve our targets.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Beyond the specific mitigation strategies, it envisions a new future where sustainability is embedded in our DNA.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Our efforts alone will not turn the tide.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Singapore contributes only around 0.1% of global emissions.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: But if we can succeed in our plans, we will show the world how a small country with severe constraints is nevertheless able to take bold action and pave the way for other countries to adopt new solutions.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: There are five pillars: City in Nature, sustainable living, energy reset, green economy and resilient future.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: They represent the priority areas in Singapore's sustainable development over the next decade.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The first pillar on City in Nature seeks to create a green, liveable and sustainable home for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Minister Desmond Lee will talk about our efforts to infuse nature into our urban fabric.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Conserving resources must become our way of life – consume less, recycle more and take public transport.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Minister Lawrence Wong will share how we will nurture future generations to be more environmentally conscious.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Minister Ong Ye Kung will speak about greening our commutes at MOT's Committee of Supply.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I will elaborate on our transition towards a zero-waste nation.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: To lower our carbon footprint, we will need to employ cleaner energy, and use it more efficiently and this is our third pillar, energy reset.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Minister Tan See Leng will speak on plans to make our energy and power systems cleaner and more efficient.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Minister Desmond Lee will share how we will make our built environment and urban spaces more sustainable and Minister Ong Ye Kung will make the case for electric vehicles.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Sustainability can be a new engine of jobs and growth as we pivot towards a green economy, the fourth pillar.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Minister Chan Chun Sing will share how we will help our enterprises seize new opportunities in sustainability and prepare Singaporeans to take on green jobs.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: With our position as the regional financial and services hub, carbon services and green financing will be new areas of growth.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This is what the fifth pillar of the Green Plan is about – building a resilient future.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Additional details will be shared in my second speech later.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: First, coastal defence, which Ms Poh Li San asked about.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Second, keeping Singapore cool in a warming world.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: According to the Meteorological Service Singapore, it is almost one degree Celsius hotter today than in the 1950s.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Apart from global warming, it is also driven by the Urban Heat Island effect, or UHI for short – a phenomenon where an urbanised area is warmer than its surroundings because of the built environment and increased human activities.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The UHI effect is a complex topic that requires in-depth studies.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will chart a science-based roadmap to holistically and decisively moderate temperature rise in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Third, strengthening Singapore's food security by growing local in a resource-efficient way.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: With climate change bringing about widespread extreme weather events and soaring global demand for food, the global food market will be more volatile and unpredictable.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And this is a critical risk for Singapore as we import over 90% of our food supply.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will do so with a keen eye on energy, water and land efficiency.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This complements our other strategies of diversifying import sources and growing food overseas to strengthen food security.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: While the five pillars of the Green Plan will map the way forward, the public, private and people sectors must come together for us to succeed, as Ms Hany Soh highlighted.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The Public Service will lead on sustainability as part of the GreenGov.SG initiative which Deputy Prime Minister announced in his Budget speech.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Second, we will expand the scope of GreenGov.SG beyond Government offices, to include other public sector infrastructure and operations.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: GreenGov.SG will encompass a far wider array of assets to include waste-to-energy plants, public transport infrastructure, hawker centres and healthcare facilities.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: With this expanded scope, the public sector will take on a greater responsibility to enhance the sustainability of our operations.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Third, we will embed sustainability practices in the public sector's core business areas and influence our service providers and suppliers to be more sustainable.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As a major consumer of goods and services, the public sector can and will influence the industry towards sustainable business choices and practices by incorporating more sustainability requirements in our procurement framework.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Fourth, we will build an organisational culture of sustainability and grow the movement amongst Public Service officers.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: More details on GreenGov.SG will be released over the course of the year.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Besides the public sector, the private sector plays a critical role in the Green Plan, as Ms Janet Ang so eloquently argued for.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
