text: Third, Minister Tan mentioned about how we are planning to import hydro power from Lao PDR and that sounds environmentally friendly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But I just wonder whether we have also studied the environmental impact of building this hydro-electric power station, how destructive it is for the environment there and for the wildlife.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I hope MTI can consider not just importing the renewable energy but making sure that it does not have that big an impact on the environment in other countries.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Indeed, Madam, I think inherent in the series of questions that Mr Louis Ng asked, are all the trade-offs that we have to balance when we try and achieve the targets that he is talking about.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: One of the things which we have to consider is whether we want to import electricity.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Other jurisdictions, for example, claimed to have to achieve this target, but actually, they are importing nuclear energy from their neighbours.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Is that something which Mr Louis Ng thinks is a good idea?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: There are different things that we need to do.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: When we are considering importing clean and green energy from other countries, there are also other considerations which we have to take into account.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The other half depends on what other people do and whether or not we are able to develop the technologies, some of which do not exist today; whether we are able to get importation of electricity; whether we are able to get carbon markets to work properly.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Those are not things which are wholly within our control.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And as Mr Louis Ng said himself, even if we did all that, we have to consider the other consequences of all those actions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: These are imponderables which we need to consider with the passage of time.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I am not in the business of bursting bubbles.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And I certainly do not want to create a bubble which future generations will have difficulty trying to meet.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We do not make promises which would cause future generations problems in trying to keep as well.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I think Mr Louis Ng would probably agree with that.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Ng asked what is the timeframe for the rest of the school sector.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is not so difficult for the school sector compared to the whole of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But beyond just putting in the infrastructure to achieve net zero, what I had highlighted earlier which I think is much more important, is to get mindsets to change.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We want to inculcate in our students from an early age the mindset of sustainability, to appreciate the importance of habits.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think that is far more important than just putting in solar panels and then putting in new technology and getting the school infrastructure to be net zero.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That we will do; I think that for schools, because it is more compact, it is relatively easier.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But getting the software, getting the understanding, the habits and the mindsets – that is an important endeavour we want to do in the school sector as well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For the import from Lao PDR, in terms of the hydro power, it is a pilot.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will consider all possible sources of renewable energy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: One of the key aspects of this thing would be that we would be getting all prospective importers to submit information on their energy sources as well as environmental studies that have been done to see what the impacts are.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And that is why at this particular point in time, it is still a pilot.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are piloting from Lao PDR, we are also piloting from Malaysia.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And as we learn more in the months and in the years ahead, we will collate and find the best way forward.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: First of all, I like to thank Senior Minister and all Ministers for giving a very detailed explanation on this issue.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I have got two questions for Minister Tan.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: He mentioned the range of switches, the regional grid switch, for example.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The first question is on the weightage of the regional grid – how many percent is it, as a whole, part of the switch, a consolidation?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Second is I am concerned about the impact on electricity prices for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Maybe you can share with us to reassure Singaporeans over the next five to 10 years, the impact on the increase in prices.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Because you mentioned that: one, the electricity prices will normalise; second, data centres and digitalisation and EV charging will come on-stream; and third, the switches on boarding, including our exposure to regional grid exposures.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, can I ask the Minister if he can share the plans to mitigate this rise in prices, if any going forward, given the possibility of convergence of these factors.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As I have stated in my speech, we are really in this trilemma.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: What I am hoping to achieve is to send a message to everyone and I hope to get the support of everyone in the House, that a fundamental pillar that underpins the entire four-switch strategy is really energy conservation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At this particular point in time, in terms of the regional power grid, they are pilots.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are also working very closely under the RIE initiative in terms of looking at the R&D of developing low carbon alternatives, and of course, going very, very long into renewable energy as well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With time, we should be able to provide this House with greater clarity and details of that strategy and how much traction we are able to gain.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: From an observer's perspective – a Singaporean looking at this – the targets are a very interesting part of the plan because with technology moving so quickly, I can imagine it is difficult to say when a certain thing can happen by.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: One was actually pertaining to a point with regard to the trade-offs that Senior Minister Teo alluded to in reply to Member Louis Ng's question about nuclear power.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I can file a Parliamentary Question on this matter as to what were the findings of the Government, but certainly in terms of clean power, nuclear power that is a source that potentially should be looked at.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, it will be helpful to know what the Government's findings were in that regard.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: My question is for the public to better understand the trade-offs, because it is a sensitive subject for the members of the public to have open areas and green lungs in the country, what sort of processes take place in Government to ensure that the trade-offs that are taken to, for example, remove a forested area, is a very careful one; and there are checks and balances in that process to make sure that all other alternatives have been considered carefully?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Could I just ask Mr Pritam Singh whether he is saying the Government should study nuclear power as an option?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But it would appear that the Government has looked into it, so it would be helpful to know what the Government's position is.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But we keep an open mind on this.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We are looking even at nuclear fusion and tokamaks.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We also have to study, and I am not sure whether this is in fact the study that the Member had referred to.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We fund a research centre for nuclear and nuclear safety in Singapore, in order to keep a watch on all these issues including nuclear safety.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Although we may not develop a nuclear power plant in Singapore, our neighbours may well do so.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, we need to understand the safety implications of nuclear power plants within a certain radius of us.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The other thing which we need to be prepared for – and this may well be the subject of the study; I do not know which study Mr Pritam Singh is referring to – is that we need to be prepared for nuclear contamination in Singapore, either through a nuclear accident somewhere in the region or by deliberate action, say a terrorist action with a dirty bomb.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We have to look at how we clean up such a device or such nuclear radioactive substances that have been dispersed in Singapore, say by terrorist action – how we collect them and how we clean them up.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We actually have plans for such a thing.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We have to think ahead and we do have plans for this.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This may well be what Mr Pritam Singh was thinking.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I do not know because I do not know the specific reference.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I had gone into significant detail in two recent Parliamentary Questions and the exchanges after that.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: One on Ulu Pandan and one on Kranji, where I set out in a lot of detail, the processes, both at the Concept and Masterplan level, as well as the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) framework that goes into the assessment of ecological and environmental impact.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, I will not go into all that detail unless the Member has specific questions on my answers in the last two rounds.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But broadly speaking, we have a long-term plan or what we call currently the Concept Plan.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I had told Members of the House that we will soon be launching a conversation to relook at the concept of Singapore, which will then input into our land use plan.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And in the Masterplan, you can see the different parcels of land, even land that is vacant or vegetated, and what the land use intention is, for that land.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But beyond that, this is an iterative process, it is a living process and the different agencies that have land use needs like transport, parks and greenery, our water body agencies, our economic agencies, our housing agencies, having consulted their respective constituencies – the interest groups, the cause-based groups, members of the public, community groups – then, discuss regularly to look at the land use and see whether to proceed with certain plans because of the needs that the agencies have forecasted, or to make some changes to the usage of different parcels of land.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The first being the conservation of cores, buffers, corridors for nature; second, species recovery and habitat enhancement; third, scientific research into ecology science and its application in our eco-systems in an urban environment; and lastly, citizen science.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And then, of course, I spoke also about the EIA framework, the processes that go into how to do an environmental impact study, when it needs to be called and the kinds of agencies that are involved, as well as the enhancement we made in October of last year to put in place Biodiversity Impact Assessment (BIA) guidelines to enhance the standards and to put in place uniform standards for BIAs, as well as to provide for enforcement through the Wildlife Act and greater transparency of environmental studies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I also talked about the new things that we have been working on including an ecological connectivity survey at a high level with researchers as well as with the nature community, as well as looking at the feasibility of centralising EIA consultancy.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I will now share MSE’s work in three areas: (a) building our climate resilience; (b) decarbonising our water sector; and (c) moving towards a Zero Waste Nation.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: COVID-19 has underscored the importance of building resilience in our systems.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We have started preparations to deal with the long-term effects of climate change.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This includes investing strategically in R&D and our infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Sea-level rise poses an existential threat to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak, Ms Poh Li San and Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin asked about our plans to protect Singapore’s coastlines against rising sea levels.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will implement coastal protection measures in phases, beginning with the more vulnerable parts of our coastlines.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This year, PUB and JTC will embark on site-specific studies at the coastlines of City-East Coast and Jurong Island.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Potential measures to be examined include sea walls, polders and nature-based solutions like mangrove planting.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In developing these plans, we will search for innovation in complementing our land use, sea space needs and the natural environment.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Some of the suggestions from Dr Lim Wee Kiak are interesting and we will take them into consideration.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Climate Change has caused more intense rainfall, and more serious and frequent flooding.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As Miss Cheryl Chan has said, it is important to develop a comprehensive and coordinated understanding of Singapore’s level of flood resilience.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: To holistically manage both inland and coastal flood risks, PUB will be developing the Coastal-Inland Flood Model this year.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This computational model will simulate flood risk events and evaluate effectiveness of coastal infrastructure designs against different climatic scenarios.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This will equip PUB with capabilities to plan and implement adaptation measures.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Ms Hazel Poa asked about PUB’s long-term measures to mitigate inland flood risks.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: When designing drains and canals, PUB considers factors such as the extent and type of development, overall terrain and design rainfall intensity.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Key projects include the Bukit Timah First Diversion Canal and Stamford Detention Tank.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Ten projects will commence this year, including drainage works at Seletar North Link and Serangoon Avenue 2 and 3.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Despite our best efforts to improve our drainage system, it is not possible to completely eliminate flash floods.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It is not practical to build ever bigger drains to meet every extreme rainfall event in land-scarce Singapore.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This is why we introduced the holistic "Source-Pathway-Receptor" approach to managing flash floods.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This addresses flood protection by arresting water at source such as detention tanks, expanding capacity of pathways such as drains and canals, and deepening capacity of receptors in low-lying areas.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As Dr Lim Wee Kiak rightly pointed out, coastal and flood protection are a long-term and large-scale effort.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The Deputy Prime Minister announced at Budget that the Government intends to issue new bonds under the proposed Significant Infrastructure Government Loan Act, or SINGA, to finance infrastructure, including for coastal and flood protection.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Global warming and rising temperature is another issue that we must grapple with.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This is compounded by the Urban Heat Island effect, or UHI for short.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: When temperature rises, we turn up air-conditioners, which in turn generate more heat in the surrounding, resulting in a vicious cycle.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Built-up areas, such as the CBD, can be more than three degree Celsius hotter than our parks.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: High temperatures can be uncomfortable for our daily activities, or increase the risk of heat injuries at the workplace, sports and military training.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked about the measures taken to reduce the UHI and heat emissions.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: First, we will measure, gather data and close our knowledge gaps on the UHI effects by deploying a network of sensors islandwide.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Second, we will develop simulation models of the UHI effects under the Cooling Singapore 2.0 Research Project.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This will help us better plan and right-site open spaces and greenery to provide comfort for our residents.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Third, we will develop and implement a UHI mitigation action plan.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This will include piloting the use of cool materials, increasing urban greenery and reducing heat emissions through district cooling.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Decarbonisation and improving energy efficiency will continue to be our focus.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if we can publish a ranking of top emitters.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We agree on the need to provide a strong impetus for companies to reduce emissions and we will continue to study how we can spur this meaningfully.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Ensuring resilient water supply has been our focus since Independence.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: With bold and innovative solutions, we have closed the water loop and reused our water endless times.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: However, our water demand will continue to rise with population and economic growth, even as climate change brings about more erratic rainfall and dry spells.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Weather-resilient sources, such as NEWater and desalination, will be key pillars of our future water strategy.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We must ensure that in achieving water sustainability, we do not become more reliant on energy and increase our carbon footprint.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In the same bold and innovative spirit that enabled us to close the water loop, MSE will strive to break new frontiers in decarbonising the water sector.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Last year, we announced the construction of one of the world's largest floating solar panel system at Tengeh Reservoir.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Ms Poh Li San asked for our plans for future floating solar panels and for improving energy efficiency of water treatment.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: PUB will complete the deployment of two floating solar panel systems at Bedok and Lower Seletar Reservoirs this year.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: PUB and EDB are also exploring potential deployments in Upper Pierce and Kranji Reservoirs respectively.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Decades of R&D efforts led to our NEWater and desalination solutions.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Today, PUB is undertaking R&D efforts to reduce energy use.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: One promising example is the Flow Reversal technology in the reverse osmosis stage of NEWater production.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This has been shown to improve NEWater recovery rate from 75% to 90% with the same energy consumption.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The Plant will be co-located with Tuas Power's existing Tembusu Multi-Utilities Complex, boosting resource synergies across energy and seawater intake and outfall structures.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Last year, we reported that work has begun on Tuas Nexus – Singapore's first integrated solid waste and used water treatment facility.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It is set for completion in phases from 2025.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It will harness synergies across the water-energy-waste nexus to maximise energy and resource recovery, enabling it to be fully energy self-sufficient and even export electricity to the grid.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Building on Tuas Nexus, NEA and PUB plan to co-locate a food waste treatment facility at Changi Water Reclamation Plant.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The co-digestion of food waste and used water sludge generates additional biogas, providing more electricity for Changi Water Reclamation Plant.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Co-location also reduces the carbon footprint, as food waste collected in the east can be sent to Changi, instead of to Tuas Nexus in the west.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: NEA expects to embark on the preliminary design study for the food waste treatment facility in the first half of this year.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Through our green waterworks, low-energy water production and low-carbon water treatment, the next chapter of our water story will be written in a green and sustainable manner.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We set ambitious targets under our Zero Waste Masterplan in 2019.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Our national goal is to achieve a 70% overall recycling rate and reduce the amount of waste sent to Semakau Landfill per capita per day by 30% by 2030.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Under the Green Plan, we aim to frontload our waste-to-landfill reduction efforts over the next five years, to achieve a 20% reduction per capita per day by 2026.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We can achieve this if everyone plays their part, consuming less, wasting less and recycling more.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: At the same time, we need a paradigm shift from a linear "take-make-throw" economy to a circular economy where waste is turned into resource and used over and over again.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We need businesses, individuals and all partners to come on board.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As Mr Louis Ng pointed out, Singapore generates about 60,000 tonnes of e-waste a year.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: E-waste contains valuable resources like precious metals, which we can recover to reduce mining of raw materials.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: However, only about 6% of the e-waste disposed of by consumers is recycled via public recycling programmes.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This is why we have introduced the Extended Producer Responsibility, or EPR framework for e-waste.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This places responsibility on producers to collect and send their products for proper end-of-life treatment at e-waste recyclers licensed by NEA.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Melvin Yong and Mr Lim Biow Chuan asked about EV batteries.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The recyclers will have to adhere to depollution requirements and meet material recovery targets.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This ensures that our e-waste does not pollute the environment and useful resources are recovered for reuse.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We recently appointed ALBA Group as the Producer Responsibility Scheme, or PRS Operator to manage the physical collection and treatment of e-waste on behalf of the producers, who will finance the scheme.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: NEA is working closely with ALBA and industry stakeholders to set up the collection infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Come July, the public can look forward to more ways to recycle e-waste.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In addition to the mandatory requirement for large retailers to offer instore collection service, we have secured support from owners of other premises, such as shopping malls and Community Clubs, to place e-waste recycling bins at publicly accessible areas within their premises.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: To ensure the success of the EPR, NEA is working with premises owners and ALBA to raise awareness.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: ALBA intends to launch a website and mobile app to provide information on the EPR, including the types of e-waste covered and the recycling locations.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Individuals, too, can drive ground-up efforts on e-waste recycling.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: She chairs the Woodlands Environmental Committee and led an initiative to install e-waste recycling bins that was well-received by residents in Woodlands.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Between October 2018 and March last year, about 338 kg of e-waste was collected.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: When you lead by example, others will be inspired to follow." Let us play our part for the environment, just like Mdm Lalitha and inspire our families and friends to do the same.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We are driving nationwide efforts to reduce and recycle food waste through outreach efforts and regulatory measures.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if these premises should also report the amount of food waste segregated.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Indeed, we are considering a framework for these premises to measure and report the amount of food waste segregated for treatment.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Aside from mandatory measures, we will closely support businesses in their efforts to close waste loops.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: NEA has been seeking applicants for its 3R Fund, a co-funding programme to support businesses in implementing waste reduction projects.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Parkway Parade received funding to install a new food waste treatment system on its premises and actively reached out to tenants to segregate their food waste to be treated.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Between 2017 and 2020, Parkway Parade successfully diverted 1,200 tonnes of food waste from disposal.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Packaging waste is our third priority waste stream.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It accounts for about one-third of domestic waste disposed of, comprising materials, such as plastic, paper, metal and glass.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The transition period will give industry time to set up the collection and recycling infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will continue to engage stakeholders and we welcome all to participate in shaping Singapore's own DRS framework.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Another important aspect in recycling packaging waste is building up our local recycling capabilities.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: More than half of our domestic packaging waste disposed of is plastics.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We are pursuing both mechanical and chemical recycling solutions, the latter which can take in contaminated plastics that are not suitable for mechanical recycling.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: NEA and Shell are jointly studying the feasibility of chemical recycling in Singapore, including the carbon savings potential of diverting plastic waste from incineration to produce pyrolysis oil, or NEWOil, as feedstock for petrochemical plants.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: One issue that has captured public attention is the excessive consumption of disposables.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This includes single-use plastics which Mr Louis Ng and Mr Dennis Tan have asked about.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Disposables have a short lifespan and contribute significantly to our carbon footprint and waste.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Under GreenGov.SG, the public service is considering measures to reduce the use of disposables and will be announcing more details later in the year.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Citizens are also actively co-creating solutions with us.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In line with the SG Together movement, we convened a Citizens' Workgroup in September last year.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Fifty-five citizens of various backgrounds jointly came up with recommendations to address the issue of excessive consumption of disposables.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: They presented their recommendations to my Ministry and NEA in January.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We are heartened by the wide range of ideas, from policies such as a mandatory carrier bag charge, to behavioural nudges such as visual cues in supermarkets.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will share our responses to the recommendations next month and publish them on the Clean and Green Singapore website.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Where feasible, we will co-deliver them with the participants and other partners.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It is our hope that all Singaporeans will have a growing consciousness to care for the environment, reduce their consumption and waste less.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In so doing, we can make sustainable living a way of life and achieve our vision of becoming a Zero Waste Nation together.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It has shown us that the current way in which we consume, our habits and the way we treat our planet is not sustainable.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: But amidst the gloom, there were also many new and hopeful beginnings.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We look forward to working with all Singaporeans to take a green leap forward in 2021 towards a sustainable, resource-efficient and climate-resilient future for our nation.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I will now hand over to Senior Minister of State Dr Amy Khor.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Mr Chairman, I will now talk about building a liveable and endearing home by safeguarding public health and sustaining hawker culture.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: COVID-19 has underscored the importance of personal and public hygiene.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Last year, we launched the SG Clean movement to urgently shore up our public health defences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Practices like hand washing have become the norm.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We passed the Environmental Public Health (Amendment) Bill to introduce mandatory baseline environmental sanitation standards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Gastroenteritis incidents affected more than 1,200 persons in 2018 and 2019.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Satisfaction levels of public cleanliness at premises like markets, hawker centres and coffeeshops remain low.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Birds, which are attracted by food remnants, continue to be a nuisance, with about 90 feedback cases on this every month.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: But it is not prudent to rely solely on scarce public resources, whether for cleaning, surveillance or enforcement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: A lasting solution requires everyone to play their part.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For example, on littering, which Mr Lim Biow Chuan raised, we have increased fines, deployed camera surveillance and reviewed the Corrective Work Order (CWO) regime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We can continue stepping up enforcement, including by sending every litterbug for CWO, but this is not sustainable for the long term.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Instead, we will work with three main stakeholder groups to build and sustain a clean Singapore – with premises owners to uphold high public health standards; with the environmental services industry to transform the sector; and with individuals to engender greater social responsibility to keep Singapore clean.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will continue to promote the adoption of good hygiene practices with the "SG Clean" Quality Mark and waive certification costs this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will implement the Environmental Sanitation or ES regime, as planned.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Under this, premises managers must meet new mandatory baseline ES standards and proactively clean their premises.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The ES Technical Committee has completed the technical guide which sets out the national baseline ES guidelines like daily cleaning frequencies for high-touch surfaces and toilets, and prescribed periodic cleaning for hard-to-reach areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The guide can be customised to develop sector-specific ES standards, such as for eldercare facilities, which will be ready from mid-2021.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Eligible participants will receive up to about 90% in course fee subsidy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Clean public toilets are critical to public health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Even with mandatory baseline standards, ageing infrastructure at some hawker centres and coffeeshop toilets remains an impediment to maintaining cleanliness.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is why we introduced the Toilet Improvement Programme (TIP), which Mr Pritam Singh asked about.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is a one-off grant, where we co-fund hawker centres and coffeeshop operators to install better fittings and adopt productivity measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Our priority is to make toilets easier to clean and maintain.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: That is why we mandated features, like toilet pedestals, with anti-stain technology and a VORTEX flushing system that says "WATER", in the same spirit as our Green Plan.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Cleaners will also be helped to work more efficiently.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Similarly, ammonia detection systems will send alerts when cleaning is needed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Mr Singh suggested to pilot the TIP at a hawker centre at a hawker centre with heavy footfall.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In fact, the mandatory components of the TIP have already been tested at NEA-managed hawker centres.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: NEA has consulted and will continue to consult the Town Councils on the TIP.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will consider their suggestions including to extend the implementation timeline of the TIP.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Mr Singh asked why we provide additional subsidies to hawker centres, which remove their smoking corners?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Protecting patrons from second hand smoke and providing patrons with clean toilets are both important public health priorities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: All new hawkers centres built after 2011 are smoke free.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We have been encouraging the remaining 27 centres with smoking corners to remove them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: A higher TIP co-funding amount can help to accelerate the shift second.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Second, we will work with the Environmental Services Industry to transform the sector, which has experienced increased demand in the current pandemic.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Since we launched the Environmental Services Industry transformation map or ESITM in 2017, the industry has made great strides to transform itself.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For instance, 800 Super have secured better contracts locally and successfully ventured overseas.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It achieved this to digitalisation and building capabilities, such as GPS fleet management systems.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Now, he offers integrated environmental solutions and boast an integrated energy and resource recovery facility that powers industrial laundry services and animal feed processing.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As suggested by Dr Lim Wee Kiak, we will support the industry to future-proof their businesses beyond COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: One, we will move away from headcount-based contracts.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This ensures clear outcomes for service buyers and encourages cleaning companies to innovate and be more productive, which in turn creates better jobs and address manpower constraints.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA will roll out a refreshed outcome-based contracting guide for the cleaning industry this month, which will encourage better service delivery through technology adoption and process improvements.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It includes an easier method to measure service outcomes and sample contract clauses to cater for contingencies such as COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Service buyers and cleaning companies can agree on deploying more resources to meet additional cleaning requirements, based on the prices that cleaning companies have quoted upfront.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This offers flexibility to adapt to changing requirements.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Two, we have extended the Productivity Solutions Grant until September 2021 to support companies to adopt automation.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Tripartite Cluster for Waste Management will develop job ladders, training requirements and wage benchmarks.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We also have initiatives for the pest management sector, which Miss Rachel Ong spoke about.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are encouraging premises and pest management companies to jointly pilot customised digital solutions through the INCUBATE programme.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, NEA and Enterprise Singapore (ESG) recently closed a joint grant call with INCUBATE partners to seek solutions for a digital platform that integrates cleaning, waste and pest data.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will also work with the sector to develop outcome-based contracting guidelines for pest management contracts, targeted to be ready by end 2021.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will grow the talent pool of pest management professionals.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA is working with IHLs and the industry to revise Continuing Education & Training and Pre-Employment Training courses, such as the joint ITE-NEA certification courses for pest management.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Lest Members have the wrong impression, pest management goes beyond catching rats, killing cockroaches and controlling the mosquito population!

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It takes serious science to deal with these pests and prevent their multiplication.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The third prong in our strategy is to foster individual responsibility around public hygiene, as Mr Gan Thiam Poh mentioned.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This involves behavioural change which is very challenging, but it is the only sustainable way forward.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Recently, I launched the Clean Tables Campaign at hawker centres, coffeeshops and food courts.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As Miss Rachel Ong asked, we are adopting new ways to spread the word.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It is an uphill task to get individuals to clear their tables – old habits die hard – but it can be done.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, at Bukit Merah Central Food Centre, the Hawkers' Association customised trays with educational messages, and worked with hawkers and table cleaners to encourage patrons to return trays.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They have achieved an exemplary tray return rate of more than 70%.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I urge other hawker centres to follow their lead.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In the coming months, we will roll out the campaign at all hawker centres, coffeeshops and foodcourts.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA will install around 75 tray return racks at hawker centres on top of the 900 today.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: At coffeeshops, 10% have tray return infrastructure and SFA will work with the remaining operators to implement localised solutions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA will monitor the campaign outcome and conduct another survey on public attitudes towards tray return.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will also consider if we need to move beyond education to some form of regulation, as some members of the public have suggested.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I will now speak on sustaining hawker culture.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Restrictions on dine-in during Circuit Breaker undoubtedly affected some hawkers, but they continued to work tirelessly to supply Singaporeans with affordable food.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To support our frontline hawker heroes, we provided five months of rental waivers and subsidies for table-cleaning and centralised dishwashing services.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Over 1,300 hawkers have also taken up the $500 grant to adopt food delivery services.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Under IMDA's Hawkers Go Digital Programme, over 5,000 hawkers received an e-payment bonus up to $1,500 each.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Despite the challenges, 2020 ended on a bright note.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Hawker Culture was successfully inscribed on the UNESCO List.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I will speak on two areas – supporting hawkers and future-proofing hawker centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Both are essential parts of our hawker culture.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: First, supporting our hawkers and sustaining the trade.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Our hawkers average age is about 60 years old.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We do need to act urgently, as Mr Leong Mun Wai said, to ensure that future generations can continue to enjoy our hawker culture.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Some do it for passion, some with ambition to eventually expand, and others to continue a family legacy.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, Mr Fabian Tan of Skirt & Dirt at Tiong Bahru Market, a 32-year-old culinary school graduate and former senior sous chef, joined the hawker trade through NEA's Incubation Stall Programme.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Fabian's goal is to eventually open his own café or restaurant.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To aspiring hawkers, we will continue to do what we can to help you start on a good footing.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: First, we introduced the Hawkers Development Programme to equip aspiring hawkers with the skills to run a successful business.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The programme comprises classroom training, apprenticeship with veteran hawkers and an incubation stage with mentorship support and training allowances.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: One example is Workgroup member Ms Sandy Tan Puay Puay, who owns Kueh Ho Jiak at Blk 6 Tanjong Pagar Plaza.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are also increasing the number of incubation stalls.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As Mr Gan highlighted, a critical factor in sustaining the trade is the transmission of culinary skills across generations.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This scheme will also facilitate the transfer of hawker stalls and recipes, by matching veteran hawkers to aspiring successors.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Leong suggested that we focus on preserving hawker recipes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Muhamad Faisal Abdul Manap asked about reviving the Hardship Scheme.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As he noted, we discontinued this in 1990 as job opportunities had increased, even for the unskilled.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The scheme also had limited effectiveness with low take-up rate, as most hardship cases preferred to wait for a vacant stall in more popular centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Today, we have many schemes to help the needy upskill and find good jobs, while providing financial assistance and other support.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: More importantly, subsidising rentals alone will not guarantee success.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Rentals are not the biggest cost for our hawkers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It is raw materials and manpower costs that make up about three-quarters of hawkers' operating costs, based on NEA's survey of our hawker centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Sustaining a hawker stall requires entrepreneurship and passion, no different from any business.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Nonetheless, we do want to support the needy who are genuinely passionate to enter the trade.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We now have schemes which are open to all, including ex-offenders.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Our Hawkers Development Programme and Incubation Stall Programme offer aspiring hawkers subsidised skills training, training allowances, rental subsidies and a fitted-out stall, including at hawker centres run by socially-conscious enterprises or SEHCs, to let them test their mettle at lower start-up costs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They can also bid for a stall through NEA's monthly tender exercise, where no minimum bids are required.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As a result, the median rental of cooked food stalls in hawker centres today, including SEHCs, is much lower than the rentals in coffeeshops or food courts.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This is part of our effort to keep operating costs low and reduce the barriers of entry for new hawkers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Coupled with the earlier-mentioned schemes, we hope this improves the viability of the trade to attract a new generation of hawkers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I will now speak on hawker centres, an important component of our hawker culture.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Leong said hawker centres have been declining in popularity.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: An NEA survey found that close to 80% of Singaporeans patronise hawker centres at least once a week.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Hence, it is opportune to consider how we can future-proof our hawker centres as Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin suggested.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: During the recent SG HawkerFest, more than 7,700 participants shared what infrastructure and features they hoped to see in future hawker centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We received many suggestions, from improving ventilation, to providing live updates on crowd levels at hawker centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The HTP will incorporate lessons from COVID-19 and sustain our hawker culture.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The programme will focus on ensuring a clean and safe environment at hawker centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, aisles and tables will be better spaced to minimise crowding.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will create a more conducive environment for patrons, hawkers and cleaners.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will also enhance the use of technology and support digitalisation efforts.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, we will work towards deploying sensors for crowd monitoring and to facilitate maintenance.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Sustainability will also be a priority, as part of our effort to bring sustainability to the community under GreenGov.SG.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The new Senja Hawker Centre will have features like food waste digestion, rainwater harvesting and solar panels.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will progressively implement the HTP at new hawker centres and centres which undergo redevelopment.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will also conduct engagements with stakeholders at a few existing hawker centres to co-create centre-level solutions for these centres, to address infrastructure gaps based on COVID-19 lessons.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We hope to learn from these "test" centres and continue to refine the HTP.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: (In Mandarin):   Our hawker centres are an important component of our hawker culture.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: During the recent SG HawkerFest, we received many suggestions on the infrastructure and features that the public hoped to see in hawker centres of the future.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The HTP will incorporate lessons from COVID-19 and sustain our thriving hawker culture from generation to generation.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, aisles and tables will be better spaced to minimise crowding.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will enhance the use of technology and support digitalisation efforts, including sensors for crowd monitoring and to facilitate maintenance.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will progressively implement the HTP at the new hawker centres, and centres which undergo redevelopment.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will also conduct engagements with stakeholders at a few existing hawker centres to co-create feasible solutions, to address infrastructure gaps based on lessons learnt from COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: (In English): Mr Gan asked about our new hawker centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Senja Hawker Centre is also scheduled to open early next year.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The SEHC model has allowed hawkers in these centres to better compete in a tough F&B landscape.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: SEHC operators curate the food options and organise events to attract more footfall.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will continue to work closely with hawkers, operators and other stakeholders to refine the model.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As is our MSE tradition, I have arranged to serve Skirt & Dirt's sliders and Kueh Ho Jiak's kueh.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Min jiang kueh from Munchi Delights and epok-epok from Kalsom Kuih Muih Curry Puff, both at Yishun Park Hawker Centre, are also back by popular demand.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Also, in the same tradition, let me also share a zero-waste tip with Members.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Today, I am wearing a necklace fashioned from old t-shirts, turning it into NewCloth, just like NEWater, NewSand and NewOil and NewFeet!

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Chairman, in conclusion, the past year has focused our attention on the importance of sustaining a liveable and endearing home, cleanliness and hygiene as our first line of defence and safeguarding our hawker culture.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: My Ministry will continue to work hard on these fronts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Chairman, MSE remains committed in ensuring our water sustainability and supply of safe food for future generations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Even as we commission new desalination and NEWater plants, this infrastructure cannot keep pace with demand as our economy and our population grow.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We must not let up on our efforts to conserve water.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng suggested tapping on technology to enhance water use efficiency.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This is what we are trying to do.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Consumers can monitor their daily water use and receive notifications and tips through the accompanying web portal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Alerts will be sent when abnormal water use patterns are detected, signifying potential leaks that need to be fixed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: As a start, only those with a minimum two-tick efficiency rating can be sold.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: PUB will also introduce the mandatory minimum water efficiency requirements for three types of commercial equipment, namely washer extractors, dishwashers and high-pressure washers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Starbucks managed to reduce its annual water consumption, as an example, by 2% for its outlets that have switched to water-efficient dishwashers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Six hundred and forty-five cubic metres of water was saved in a year, equivalent to about a quarter of an Olympic-sized swimming pool, and they also saved $1,800 from their annual bills.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: PUB will install 1,200 permanent leak detection sensors by 2021 to remotely monitor approximately 500 km of large water pipelines.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Advanced leak detection tools, such as the SmartBall, will be propelled by the water flow within the pipeline to survey long stretches for leaks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng stressed the importance of safeguarding our used water resources.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Singapore is one of the few countries to close the water loop, returning used water to the system in the form of NEWater as well as industrial water.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: PUB takes a zero-tolerance approach towards improper used water discharges and will not hesitate to prosecute errant companies because improper discharges pose health hazards to sewerage workers and cause disruptions to our water reclamation process.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: PUB's enforcement efforts are complemented by advanced sensing technologies to monitor these illegal discharges.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: The network of online volatile organic compounds monitoring units will be expanded from the current 40 units to 100 units by end-2021.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: One hundred and seventy-five trade premises will have microbial electrochemical sensors installed in their last inspection chambers, from 100 today, to alert PUB when excessive heavy metals are detected.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: These data help PUB more accurately identify high-risk trade premises and address emerging problems early.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore has developed a multi-pronged approach to ensure our food security, including import diversification, local production and stockpiling of essential food items.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: We also support local companies to expand overseas and export their produce back home.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: In 2019, we announced our 30 by 30 goal to buffer Singapore from global disruptions arising from climate change.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: While one farm has since withdrawn and another has yet to accept the offer, the other seven remain on track.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: One successful recipient, Indoor Farm Factory Innovation is setting up a high-tech indoor vegetable farm with a vertical integration growth system of up to eight meters in height.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: I look forward to their vegetables hitting the shelves this year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: To produce more with less, we must continue investing in technology.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Under the $144 million Singapore Food Story R&D Programme, three Grant Calls on Sustainable Urban Food Production and Future Foods on Alternative Proteins have been launched.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: SFA has supported existing farms to achieve higher productivity through the Agriculture Productivity Fund (APF) since 2015.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: As of end-December 2020, $43 million have been committed from the APF to support 118 companies and farms.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Homegrown company, Blue Ocean Aquaculture Technology, benefited from the APF to invest in the Recirculating Aquaculture System technology which enables it to farm fish in an indoor controlled environment and to recycle water within the production loop.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: On Ms Nadia Samdin’s question, the ACT Fund has been designed with several improvements over the APF.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: It will better cater to farms of different scales and development needs, from start-up to growth and expansion.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: It will have a higher co-funding quantum and wider scope in support of farms that adopt advanced farming systems which improve productivity and resource efficiency.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: SFA has also made more spaces available for our local farms.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Five tranches of agri-land tendered out will progressively be operational in the coming years, and the first batch of Multi-Storey Carpark (MSCP) rooftop farms will commence production this year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Seven more HDB MSCP rooftops are currently being tendered for urban farming, while the tender for our sixth tranche of land sales will be awarded in the coming weeks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: To ensure that we optimise our limited agri-land, SFA will masterplan around 390 hectares in Lim Chu Kang to create a vibrant agri-food hub that will anchor global and local best-in-class companies in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: As Mr Don Wee suggested, we should co-create the masterplan with stakeholders including the food and non-food farms, nature groups, residents around the area.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: I have kickstarted a series of conversations with these stakeholders to better understand their needs and their aspirations for Lim Chu Kang, and we will continue these conversations through the year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: With their feedback, we will also form dedicated workgroups to develop the masterplan, and these will be incorporated with the findings of the environmental baseline and topographical studies, when we launch the masterplanning consultancy in end-2021.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: We hear Mr Don Wee’s concerns about the impact to the livelihoods of affected farmers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: We will continue to facilitate their transition plans, including feasibility of moving to indoor spaces.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: SFA will work with the industry to minimise any disruption to local production during this transition.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Ms Nadia Samdin asked about the plans to unlock the potential of our local sea-based farms.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Most of the approximately 100 coastal farms in the Straits of Johor adopt open-net cage farming techniques.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: SFA has been encouraging them to invest in technology to enhance productivity and resilience against external environmental risks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Farms are also encouraged to use fish feed that minimises impact on the marine eco-system, and tap on solar and tidal energy to power their farming systems.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Farms can apply for the ACT Fund for their capital investments.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: And following feedback from farms, SFA will launch new sea space tenders on leases within the next few years to provide farms with greater certainty on the use of sea spaces.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: To ensure that our sea spaces can sustain high-yielding production over the long term, SFA will work with the farms to monitor the impact of aquaculture activities on farming sites and measures to manage the spread of fish diseases.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: SFA has engaged the industry to understand their concerns and we strive to uplift the sector, build food resilience and generate good jobs for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: I echo Miss Cheryl Chan, Dr Lim Wee Kiak and Ms Nadia Samdin’s calls to build a new generation of agri-food skilled workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: SFA is working with Institutes of Higher Learning and local farms on courses and structured internship programmes to equip students and adult job seekers with skillsets directly relevant to the agri-food sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: (In Mandarin):   MSE endeavors to strengthen the production capability of our local farms and facilitate the transformation of the agri-food sector to ensure enough food supply for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: This will help enhance our food resilience and create good business opportunities and jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: In addition, we will also work with local sea-based farms on ways to keep our sea spaces highly productive over the long term, including investing in advanced farming systems and monitoring impact of their activities on farming sites.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: To provide farms with greater certainty on the use of sea space, SFA will launch new sea space tenders on leases within the next few years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: (In English): As our farms build capabilities and increase production, consumers can make a conscious choice to support local produce, which is fresher and lasts longer.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: SFA launched the SG Fresh Produce logo in 2020 to facilitate consumers in identifying local produce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: A new “Clean & Green” standard for urban farms will be introduced this year, as a mark of assurance that produce is free from synthetic pesticides and grown in a clean farming environment using resource-efficient and sustainable practices.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: SFA will pilot two projects recommended by the Citizens’ Workgroup, where hospitals feature local produce in new mothers’ first meal after delivery, and wet markets will make it easier for consumers to identify local produce at the stalls.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: While most farms produce for the domestic market, SFA and ESG are also assisting them to secure market access overseas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: As mentioned by Ms Nadia Samdin, the formation of SFA in 2019 brought various food-related functions under a single agency, allowing SFA to have better regulatory oversight of the entire food supply chain from farm to fork.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: To manage new and emerging food safety risks as the agri-food landscape develops, SFA will introduce a new Bill this year to consolidate and strengthen its powers that currently reside in several pieces of legislation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: With more novel food products being developed, Mr Gan Thiam Poh is spot-on in suggesting that more food safety assurances should be put in place.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: SFA will also inspect and sample novel food products for testing, as is being done for other food products.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: However, food safety is a joint responsibility with the industry and consumers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Food companies must ensure that their products are safe and fit for consumption.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: And to help consumers make informed food choices, the new Act will continue to impose existing requirements for companies to label the product packaging to indicate the true nature of the food.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: As pointed out by Ms Nadia Samdin, another trend accelerated by the pandemic is the proliferation of food delivery.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Mr Chairman, I urge Members to support the work done by MSE, PUB and SFA, and to secure Singapore’s food and water supplies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Assurances on food and water security serve as social and psychological ballasts for Singapore as we build back better.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Speaker, just to clarify the consultancy study I referred to in my question to Senior Minister Teo, it was an NEA study on the development of storage sites for radioactive contaminated waste, not nuclear.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I said nuclear, I should have said radioactive.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: These are all very game-changing circular energy and self-sufficient strategies to ensure our water supply in the long run is secure.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Heng announced in his Budget speech that Green Bonds worth $19 billion of sustainability focus projects would be set aside such as for the Tuas Nexus project.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: MSE will support efforts to promote the industry in sustainability.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: But fundamentally, we must make sure that our large infrastructure must meet our needs.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will want our infrastructure to also meet our sustainability goals.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: With that, as the basic assumptions, we will be happy to work with any agencies to promote sustainability services, including financial reporting and verification.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: First, I would like to thank Senior Minister Teo and all the Ministers, the Senior Minister of State and Ministers of State for all their informative and exciting speeches.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: One on hawker culture and one on the electric vehicle.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: First, on the hawker culture, I would like to ask the Senior Minister of State Amy Khor, with the declining number of hawkers expected in the future does she think it is viable to continue to increase the number of hawker centres?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I am a bit worried that in the future, we may have a scenario whereby our hawker centres are no longer serving local food, but more and more foreign food.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So is that a scenario that is acceptable if that happens?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Second question on the electric vehicle, what kind of changes in electricity demand pattern are we expecting with the EV introduction and how are we changing our grid system to cater for that?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In other words, can our grid system cope with the surge in electricity demand?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And together with that, is there going to be a very significant increase in electricity prices going forward due to this structural change?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Of course, we have the cyclical change in the oil price and all that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But with the change to the introduction of EVs, there will be a structural change in our energy market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Will that lead to a significant rise in electricity price?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And every month, when we tender, there will always be bidders for these stalls.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Through our various programmes to attract a new generation of hawkers to run the hawker stalls, we also actually have many applicants.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We also have many requests from actually many Members of this House for a hawker centre.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, as I have said, the Member is not correct to say that hawker centres are declining in popularity.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With regard to the food, recently, we had our hawker culture listed in the UNESCO Representative List and we need to sustain, and we want to sustain, the hawker trade as well as safeguard our hawker culture.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To do this, we also need to ensure that the food served, as well as the environment of the hawker centre, evolves according to the needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Increasingly, all kinds of food will be served cosmopolitan because we are a cosmopolitan, multicultural, multiracial country.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, I do not think we need to be too concerned about this.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: What we need to do is ensure that our hawker centres continue to provide affordable delicious food in a clean environment.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With regard to heritage food, we also have programmes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I think the fact that hawker culture is the pride of everyone in Singapore, there is great hope that we will be able to sustain it together.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If let us say, by 2040, the entire vehicle population runs on electricity, and needs to be charged, this is what we call an energy reset.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, instead of every vehicle having a little combustion engine and generating power, you now feed them with electricity and then you generate the power centrally somewhere else.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That is equivalent to one to two generating units.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And one to two generating units are equivalent to 8% to 16% of the current generation power.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, that is what we meant by an energy reset if we move the entire vehicle population to electricity.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But it is a much more efficient way of generating power and will reduce carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If there is a demand, you will attract plantings, you will attract investments.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So long as there are plantings of new generation units, you fundamentally do not change the supply and demand conditions in the market.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Of course, there is downstream impact that Mr Leong Mun Wai asked, which is the grid infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I mentioned just now that so long as we do not insist on fast charging, the upgrade of the infrastructure is towards the last mile, which is not huge.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If we can live with slower and overnight charging, it is not a huge investment.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And all these services are already happening in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, the right comparison is, compared to paying for diesel and petrol, it is actually a lot more attractive and competitive.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: I have a clarification for Minister of State Desmond Tan.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: What is the impact of the minimum water efficiency labelling scheme on the industry, and whether existing equipment needs to be replaced with the two ticks when the minimum water efficiency labelling scheme kicks in?

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Member for the question.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: In fact, it is expected to be saving water and also save costs for the consumers as well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: So, maybe I will just break it down into two parts because the first part is about the water closet flush valves which will only affect industry and not the residential part.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: So, in this respect, there is minimal impact to the industry as there are sufficient models out there that meet the minimum standard today.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: And water-efficient models are also not more costly than the less water-efficient ones.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: So, there is no requirement for all existing flushes to be replaced.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: On the commercial equipment side, we have also done a study in consultation with the industry and, likewise, the impact is not high because there are sufficient models out there.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: And the cost, in fact, for the more water-efficient ones are even lower than their less water-efficient counterparts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Likewise, there is no requirement to replace all existing equipment washers if you do not meet the current requirement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: It is only for those who are either replacing new ones or intending to buy new equipment.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I just have one more question to seek clarification from Minister Ong.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because this is also a question from the residents and also I have not enough technical knowledge.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: What he saying is that if, at night, everybody starts to charge the battery for the car, would it not lead to a sudden surge in the demand and then if it causes blackout or things like that, something similar to like sometimes, at night, you cannot get access to the Internet properly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, can the Minister enlighten us on this?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Chairman, I think to answer Mr Leong's question, it is, indeed, a function of supply and demand.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: What we are doing in terms of the grid is to expand and upgrade the grid.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And as I have alluded to earlier in my speech, we will pace it out and we have quite a number of years to invest and to expand and also to upgrade the grid.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Of course, if everyone chooses to go into charging their vehicles over a very set period of time, then that peak will go up to about 16%.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think that was the point that Minister Ong talked about.The range is between 8% and 16%.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, there are plans that are needed for between one 600 megawatt generator to two 600 megawatt generators to generate that peak power that is required.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Louis Ng, can you very quickly withdraw your amendment?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Sorry, Chairman, I just want to add one point.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If people start to charge their vehicles at night when we all sleep, it is actually quite welcomed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is at night that the usage is generally lower.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the day time, there are lots of economic activities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, if some of these economic activities move to the night, you are charging, actually it smoothens out the generation capacity.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Dennis Tan, do you have a question?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Just a quick clarification for either Minister Chan or Minister Ong.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: In the Budget debate speech, I said I understand the Government has been studying the potential of battery swapping as a complement to EV charging.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I am just wondering whether the Government can provide the House with some update on its study so far.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think we do not rule out any technology.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: From the current trend, it has become quite clear.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, if you look at whether it is US, Europe, China, they are all going quite big now on electricity charging.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Tesla is probably, I believe, the fastest selling EV in the world now and you cannot swap a Tesla battery.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is the entire plate and chassis of the car.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Louis Ng, would you like to withdraw your amendment?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But I believe we had one of the longest COS and I also believe MSE is one of the most loved Ministry because we focus on something that Singaporeans love – food.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: And I know the hawker fare is waiting for us.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: So, on that note, Sir, I beg leave to withdraw the amendment.

text: I feel compelled to take a break now.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will give ourselves an extra five minutes.
